title: AP Psychology
subtitle: The science of mind and behavior
note: Aligned to the College Board Course and Exam Description, Course Framework V.1 (2024 redesign).

units.title: Science Practices and Research Methods
units.blurb: How psychologists ask questions and defend answers with evidence.

topics.title: Research Foundations · Science Practice 2

lessons.title: Scientific Attitudes & the Scientific Method
lessons.overview: Unit launch + the three scientific attitudes (curiosity, skepticism, humility), why psychology counts as a science and the founders who built it, and how to distinguish critical thinking from pseudoscience using the Mozart-effect case.
objectives: Describe curiosity, skepticism, and humility and explain how each makes psychology a self-correcting science.
Distinguish science from pseudoscience using falsifiability and the diagnostic markers, applied to a real case.
essentialQuestions: How does a scientific attitude differ from everyday opinion?
Why does psychology count as a science, and how do we tell science from pseudoscience?

source.title: The Fallacy of Personal Validation (abstract, paraphrased)
source.author: Bertram R. Forer

lessons.title: Research Methods Toolkit: Which Method Answers Which Question
lessons.overview: The six research methods and the decision rule that matches each to its question, the experiment as the only causal method (Bandura 1961; Milgram 1963), the descriptive methods and correlation, and how the wrong method (Wakefield 1998) gets a true question wrong.
objectives: Match a research question to the appropriate method and name each method's strength and weakness.
Explain why only an experiment licenses a causal claim, and identify the IV, DV, and control group.
essentialQuestions: Which research method answers which kind of question?
What is each method good at: and where does each fail?

source.title: Meta-Analysis of Psychotherapy Outcome Studies (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Mary Lee Smith & Gene V. Glass

lessons.title: Experiments, Variables & Confounds
lessons.overview: The anatomy of a true experiment (IV, DV, operational definitions, random assignment), the four confounds that masquerade as causes (placebo, demand, experimenter bias, spontaneous remission), the blinding ladder, and STAR*D as a real large-scale RCT.
objectives: Identify the IV, DV, and operational definition in an experiment and explain how random assignment supports causal inference.
Detect confounds and explain how a control group and double-blinding remove them.
essentialQuestions: What makes an experiment causal: and what makes it NOT?
How do confounds and blinding decide whether we can trust a result?

source.title: STAR*D, Acute and Longer-Term Outcomes in Depressed Outpatients (abstract, adapted)
source.author: A. John Rush et al.

lessons.title: Correlation, Sampling & Generalizability
lessons.overview: Correlation (r, direction, strength) and its three rivals to causation, the four sampling methods, the crucial random-sampling-vs-random-assignment distinction, and the WEIRD problem plus statistical power as limits on generalizability.
objectives: Interpret a correlation's sign and strength and explain why correlation cannot establish causation.
Distinguish sampling methods and explain how random sampling (generalizability) differs from random assignment (causation).
essentialQuestions: What can a correlation tell us: and what can it never tell us?
When do lab findings apply to the real world?

source.title: Adolescent Well-Being and Digital-Technology Use (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Amy Orben & Andrew K. Przybylski

lessons.title: Descriptive & Inferential Statistics
lessons.overview: Descriptive statistics (mean/median/mode, SD), the normal curve and the 68-95-99.7 rule, inferential statistics (null hypothesis, p-values, Type I/II errors), and effect size as the answer to 'how big?' beyond the p-value.
objectives: Choose and interpret appropriate descriptive statistics and apply the 68-95-99.7 rule to a normal distribution.
Interpret p-values, Type I/II errors, and effect size, and explain why significance is not the same as importance.
essentialQuestions: How do psychologists decide whether a finding is real?
Why is 'statistically significant' not the same as 'practically important'?

source.title: Positive-Psychology Interventions, a Meta-Analysis (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Linda Bolier et al.

lessons.title: Ethics, Historical Harms & the IRB
lessons.overview: Research ethics: the five APA pillars, the historical harms that produced each rule (Tuskegee, Milgram, Little Albert, Zimbardo, MKULTRA, Holmesburg), and the Belmont Report + IRB system that operationalized reform, applied to the Kramer 2014 Facebook study. Carries the sensitivity strip + crisis lines.
objectives: Explain the five APA ethics pillars and the three Belmont principles and tie each to a historical harm.
Evaluate a study's ethics, identifying violations and the IRB-required changes that would fix them.
essentialQuestions: How did psychology's ethics code emerge from its worst mistakes?
What must a study include to pass ethical review today?

source.title: Experimental Evidence of Massive-Scale Emotional Contagion (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Adam D. I. Kramer, Jamie E. Guillory & Jeffrey T. Hancock

lessons.title: Unit 0 Synthesis & Research Literacy Drill
lessons.overview: A synthesis + research-literacy drill: a six-target integrator (method, IV, DV, sample, statistics, limitation) applied to four real abstracts (Cohen 1991; Ainsworth 1978; Bond & Smith 1996; Jones & Harris 1967), with the two stalking AP traps, sampling vs. assignment and correlation vs. causation. Unit 0 Test prep.
objectives: Decode a research abstract for method, variables, sample, statistics, and a specific limitation or ethical issue.
Apply the six-target integrator across study types and avoid the sampling-vs-assignment and correlation-vs-causation traps.
essentialQuestions: Can you read a research abstract like a scientist?
How do method, sample, statistics, and ethics combine into one judgment about a study?

source.title: Psychological Stress and Susceptibility to the Common Cold (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Sheldon Cohen, David Tyrrell & Andrew Smith

vocab.def: The habits of curiosity, skepticism, and humility that make inquiry empirical and self-correcting.
Demanding evidence before accepting a claim; not cynicism, but 'How do we know?'
Willingness to revise a belief in light of disconfirming evidence; data over ego.
The property that a claim could, in principle, be disproven (Popper 1959); the line between science and pseudoscience.
A claim that mimics scientific language but resists testing and disconfirmation.
The tendency to accept vague, general personality statements as uniquely true of oneself (Forer 1948).
The factor the experimenter deliberately manipulates.
The outcome the experimenter measures; it 'depends on' the IV.
A number from -1.00 to +1.00 giving the direction and strength of a relationship; it does not establish cause.
An in-depth study of one person or small group; rich detail but N = 1, not generalizable.
Recording behavior in its natural setting without manipulation; high realism, no causal inference.
A quantitative synthesis that pools effect sizes across many studies; only as good as the studies it pools.
A concrete, replicable statement of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
A variable other than the IV that systematically differs between groups and could explain the DV.
Improvement caused by the expectation of treatment rather than the treatment itself.
Cues that let participants infer the hypothesis and change their behavior accordingly (Orne 1962).
The researcher's expectations unintentionally influencing participants or measurement (Rosenthal 1966).
A design in which neither participants nor data-collectors know who is in which condition.
The entire group of interest that a claim is meant to describe.
The subset of the population actually studied.
A procedure giving every member of the population an equal chance of selection; supports generalizability.
A non-probability sample of whoever is easy to reach; fast but rarely representative.
The degree to which findings extend from the sample to the broader population.
The probability that a study detects a real effect when one exists; rises with sample size (Cohen 1988).
Three measures of central tendency: the average, the middle value, and the most frequent value.
A measure of how tightly scores cluster around the mean.
A symmetric bell-shaped distribution following the 68-95-99.7 rule.
The probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis were true.
A false positive (rejecting a true null) / a false negative (missing a real effect).
A standardized measure of the magnitude of an effect, independent of sample size.
Participants' agreement to take part after being told the study's purpose, risks, benefits, and right to withdraw.
A participant's freedom to leave a study at any time without penalty.
A full post-study explanation, especially after deception, with a chance to withdraw one's data.
A panel that reviews and must approve human-subjects research before data collection.
The federal report establishing respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as research principles.
Pressuring participation through excessive payment, authority, or social pressure, violating voluntary consent.
The ability to decode a study's method, variables, sample, statistics, and ethics from an abstract.
The degree to which a study supports a causal claim, protected by random assignment and control.
The degree to which findings generalize beyond the sample, supported by representative sampling.
Overweighting dispositional and underweighting situational causes of others' behavior (Jones & Harris 1967).
A monotonic relationship in which higher levels of a variable produce larger effects.
A variable that changes the strength or direction of a relationship (e.g., culture in Bond & Smith 1996).

misconceptions: That psychology is a science because of its subject matter rather than its method.
That skepticism means doubting everything; it actually means calibrating belief to evidence.
That a published or popular claim is automatically valid, replication, not publication, validates findings.
That a strong correlation proves causation.
That a vivid case study or a large survey can establish cause.
That publication in a journal validates a causal claim (replication does).
That random assignment and random sampling are the same thing.
That a high improvement rate proves a treatment works without a control group.
That 'open-label' results are as trustworthy as double-blind results.
That a large sample is automatically representative (bias beats volume).
That random sampling and random assignment do the same job.
That a strong correlation in a survey can support a causal claim.
That 'p < .05' means there is a 95% chance the effect is real, or that it measures effect size.
That 'no significant difference' proves there is no effect (it may be a Type II error from low power).
That the mean is always the best summary, even for skewed data.
That a Terms-of-Service or EULA click counts as informed consent.
That deception is always unethical (it is permitted with minimal risk and a full debrief).
That large payment is always a neutral incentive rather than potential coercion.
That a meta-analysis is itself an experiment (it inherits the validity of its input studies).
That a high correlation (e.g., r = .78) proves causation.
That a 'limitation' can be generic rather than tied to a specific design feature.

units.title: Biological Bases of Behavior
units.blurb: The body's hardware: genes, neurons, brain, sleep, and the senses.

topics.title: Interaction of Heredity and Environment

lessons.title: Why Biology in a Psychology Course? Heredity, Environment & Evolution
lessons.overview: Unit launch + the nature/nurture interaction, the evolutionary perspective (and the eugenics caution), and the twin/family/adoption methods used to study genetic influence on behavior.
objectives: Explain the interaction of heredity and environment in shaping behavior and mental processes.
Describe the evolutionary perspective and identify how twin, family, and adoption studies investigate genetic influence.
essentialQuestions: Why do we study biology in a psychology course?
How much of who you are is shaped by nature, and how much by nurture?

source.title: On the Origin of Species (closing passage)
source.author: Charles Darwin

vocab.def: Genetic or predisposed characteristics that influence physical, behavioral, and mental traits.
External factors a person experiences, such as family, education, and culture.
Approach explaining how natural selection shapes survival- and reproduction-promoting behavior.
Process by which traits that aid survival and reproduction become more common over generations.
Discredited, unethical attempt to 'improve' a population by discriminating against groups deemed unfit.
Research designs that compare relatives to separate hereditary from environmental influence.

misconceptions: That a behavior is purely 'genetic' or purely 'learned' rather than an interaction of both.
That natural selection or 'survival of the fittest' justifies ranking or discriminating among people.

topics.title: Overview of the Nervous System

lessons.title: Overview of the Nervous System, Central, Peripheral & Fight-or-Flight
lessons.overview: The organization of the human nervous system: CNS vs. PNS, the somatic and autonomic divisions, and the opposing sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest') branches.
objectives: Differentiate the subsystems of the human nervous system and their functions.
Explain how the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems arouse and calm the body.
essentialQuestions: How is the body's information network organized?
What happens in your body the instant you face danger, and what calms you back down?

source.title: Bodily Changes in Pain, Hunger, Fear and Rage
source.author: Walter B. Cannon

vocab.def: The brain and spinal cord; processes information and interacts with all body systems.
Nerves outside the CNS that relay messages to and from the rest of the body.
PNS division controlling voluntary skeletal-muscle movement.
PNS division controlling involuntary processes (heartbeat, digestion).
Autonomic branch that arouses the body for 'fight or flight.'
Autonomic branch that calms the body for 'rest and digest.'

misconceptions: That the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems work at the same time in the same direction (they oppose each other).
That all body processes are under voluntary (somatic) control.

topics.title: The Neuron and Neural Firing

lessons.title: The Neuron & Neural Communication
lessons.overview: The structure of the neuron (dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin, terminals), the types of neurons and glial cells, how a neuron receives excitatory/inhibitory input, and how neurons communicate chemically across the synapse.
objectives: Identify the parts of a neuron and the role of glial cells, and trace a signal's path through the cell.
Explain how neurons communicate across the synapse using neurotransmitters, receptors, and reuptake.
essentialQuestions: What are the parts of a neuron, and what does each one do?
How does one nerve cell pass a message to the next?

source.title: An Accidental Discovery, proving neurons communicate by chemistry
source.author: Otto Loewi (Nobel laureate, 1936)

lessons.title: The Action Potential & the Reflex Arc
lessons.overview: How a neuron fires: resting potential and threshold, the all-or-none action potential (depolarization), the refractory period, and the three-neuron reflex arc that protects the body faster than conscious thought.
objectives: Explain the all-or-none action potential, including resting potential, threshold, depolarization, and the refractory period.
Trace the three-neuron reflex arc and explain why it produces a response before the brain registers the stimulus.
essentialQuestions: How does a neuron actually 'fire' a message down its axon?
Why does your hand pull off a hot stove before you even feel the pain?

source.title: Description of the all-or-none law in nerve fibers
source.author: Keith Lucas / E. D. Adrian (early neurophysiology)

lessons.title: Neurotransmitters
lessons.overview: The chemical messengers of the brain: excitatory vs. inhibitory transmission and the eight AP-listed neurotransmitters (dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, GABA, glutamate, norepinephrine, endorphins, substance P), with their functions and the behaviors that change when they are out of balance.
objectives: Distinguish excitatory from inhibitory neurotransmission and explain reuptake.
Identify the eight AP-listed neurotransmitters and the behaviors/disorders associated with each.
essentialQuestions: How do specific brain chemicals shape mood, movement, and memory?
What happens when there is too much or too little of one neurotransmitter?

source.title: Dopamine and the brain's reward and movement systems (public-health summary)
source.author: U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA)

lessons.title: Hormones & Psychoactive Drugs
lessons.overview: Chemical messengers beyond the synapse: the five AP-listed hormones (adrenaline, melatonin, leptin, ghrelin, oxytocin) and how psychoactive drugs (agonists, antagonists, reuptake inhibitors) work, the four drug classes, tolerance, addiction, and withdrawal, taught with a sensitivity strip and crisis resources.
objectives: Identify the AP-listed hormones and explain how hormones differ from neurotransmitters.
Explain how psychoactive drugs (agonists, antagonists, reuptake inhibitors) and the four drug classes affect behavior, including tolerance, addiction, and withdrawal.
essentialQuestions: How do hormones in the bloodstream shape behavior differently from neurotransmitters?
How do psychoactive drugs hijack the body's own chemical messengers?

source.title: Description of stimulant effects on the nervous system
source.author: U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA)

vocab.def: A nerve cell that transmits information; the building block of the nervous system.
Support cells that provide structure, insulation, and waste transport for neurons.
Dendrites receive incoming messages; the axon carries the signal away from the cell body.
Fatty insulation around the axon that speeds the neural impulse.
The gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters carry a message.
The sending neuron's reabsorption of leftover neurotransmitter from the synapse.
A neuron's charged, ready state before it fires.
The level of stimulation required to trigger a neural impulse.
The brief electrical impulse that travels down a neuron's axon when it fires.
A neuron either fires fully or not at all; intensity is coded by firing frequency.
Brief recovery phase after firing during which a neuron cannot fire again.
Spinal-cord pathway (sensory → inter → motor neuron) producing an automatic response.
Chemical messenger released by a neuron that excites or inhibits the next neuron.
Excitatory messages make firing more likely; inhibitory make it less likely.
Movement & reward; mood & sleep; muscle movement & memory.
GABA is the main inhibitory (calming) transmitter; glutamate the main excitatory (learning) one.
Neurotransmitter affecting alertness and arousal.
Endorphins relieve pain (natural painkillers); substance P transmits pain signals.
Chemical released into the bloodstream that influences behavior and mental processes body-wide.
Adrenaline fuels fight-or-flight; melatonin regulates the sleep-wake cycle.
Leptin signals fullness; ghrelin signals hunger; oxytocin supports bonding.
Agonists encourage neural firing; antagonists block it.
A drug that blocks reabsorption, leaving more neurotransmitter active in the synapse.
Needing more for the same effect; compulsive use; symptoms when use stops.

misconceptions: That neurons physically touch to pass messages (they communicate chemically across a synaptic gap).
That a signal can travel either direction in a neuron (it flows dendrites → cell body → axon → terminals).
That a stronger stimulus makes a neuron fire 'harder' (it fires more frequently, not more strongly).
That reflexes require a conscious decision by the brain.
That only a SHORTAGE of a neurotransmitter causes problems (excess can too, e.g., dopamine dysregulation).
That every neurotransmitter does roughly the same thing (each has distinct, testable functions).
That hormones and neurotransmitters are unrelated (hormones act similarly but travel through the blood, more slowly and widely).
That all drugs either 'speed up' or 'slow down' the brain, hallucinogens distort perception instead.

topics.title: The Brain

lessons.title: The Brain I: From Brainstem to Limbic System
lessons.overview: The brain from the bottom up: the life-sustaining brainstem (medulla), the reticular activating system and reward center, the cerebellum, the limbic system (thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, amygdala), and the four cortical lobes.
objectives: Explain how the brainstem, cerebellum, and limbic structures apply to behavior and mental processes.
Locate the four cortical lobes and state each lobe's primary function.
essentialQuestions: Which parts of the brain keep you alive, balanced, and emotional?
How can damage to one small structure change behavior so dramatically?

source.title: Recovery from the Passage of an Iron Bar through the Head (the Phineas Gage case)
source.author: Dr. John Martyn Harlow

lessons.title: The Brain II: Split-Brain Research, Language & Plasticity
lessons.overview: What happens when the hemispheres are disconnected: split-brain research (Sperry & Gazzaniga), hemispheric specialization and contralateral organization, the language areas (Broca's and Wernicke's) and aphasia, brain plasticity, and the tools (EEG, fMRI, lesioning, case studies) used to study the brain.
objectives: Explain split-brain research, hemispheric specialization, and the brain's language areas.
Define brain plasticity and identify methods (EEG, fMRI, lesioning, case studies) used to study the brain.
essentialQuestions: What happens when the two halves of the brain can no longer talk to each other?
Can a damaged brain heal or rewire itself?

source.title: Hemisphere Deconnection and Unity in Conscious Awareness
source.author: Roger W. Sperry

vocab.def: Controls basic survival functions such as breathing and heart rate.
Hindbrain structure governing coordination, balance, and some procedural learning.
Sensory relay station routing incoming senses (except smell) to the cortex.
Limbic structure that forms new long-term memories.
Limbic structure that processes fear and aggression.
Wrinkled outer brain layer divided into two hemispheres and four lobes.
Fiber band connecting and relaying information between the brain's two hemispheres.
Studies of patients whose corpus callosum was severed, revealing hemispheric specialization.
Left frontal region controlling speech production; damage causes halting speech.
Left temporal region controlling language comprehension; damage causes fluent but meaningless speech.
The brain's ability to reorganize and form new connections, aiding recovery.
fMRI images active brain areas via blood flow; EEG records electrical brain waves.

misconceptions: That the brainstem handles thinking (it handles basic survival functions).
That damage to one structure wipes out all functions (deficits are often specific).
That people are simply 'left-brained' or 'right-brained' (specialization is partial, not a personality type).
That a damaged adult brain can never recover function (plasticity allows some reorganization).

topics.title: Sleep

lessons.title: Sleep: Circadian Rhythms, Stages & the Sleeping Brain
lessons.overview: Consciousness and the sleeping brain: the circadian rhythm (and what disrupts it), the NREM stages identified by EEG, hypnagogic sensations, the 90-minute cycle, and paradoxical REM sleep with REM rebound.
objectives: Explain how the sleep/wake cycle (circadian rhythm) affects behavior and mental processes.
Identify the stages of sleep by their EEG patterns and describe REM (paradoxical) sleep.
essentialQuestions: What is your brain doing while you sleep?
Why do you feel groggy after crossing time zones or working a night shift?

source.title: Regularly Occurring Periods of Eye Motility … During Sleep (discovery of REM)
source.author: Eugene Aserinsky & Nathaniel Kleitman

lessons.title: Why We Sleep: Dream Theories, Sleep's Purpose & Sleep Disorders
lessons.overview: Why we dream and why we sleep: the activation-synthesis and consolidation theories of dreaming, sleep's restorative and memory functions and the costs of deprivation, and the five AP-listed sleep disorders.
objectives: Compare the activation-synthesis and consolidation theories of dreaming.
Explain the restorative and memory functions of sleep and identify common sleep disorders.
essentialQuestions: Why do we dream, and why do we sleep at all?
What happens to the mind and body when sleep goes wrong?

source.title: Why We Sleep, the case for sleep and memory (summary of consolidation research)
source.author: Matthew Walker (sleep scientist)

vocab.def: Awareness of one's internal and external world; includes sleep and wakefulness.
The body's roughly 24-hour biological cycle, including sleep and wakefulness.
Non-REM sleep (Stages 1-3) that deepens early and shortens across the night.
Rapid-eye-movement, 'paradoxical' sleep with wake-like brain waves and vivid dreaming.
Brief sensory experiences (e.g., a falling sensation) when entering Stage 1 sleep.
The increase in REM sleep that follows a period of REM deprivation.
Theory that dreams are the brain's interpretation of random REM neural activity.
View that sleep/dreaming serves to organize and store memories.
Persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep.
Disorder marked by sudden, uncontrollable episodes of sleep.
Disorder of repeated pauses in breathing during sleep.
Sleepwalking; occurs during deep NREM sleep.

misconceptions: That the brain 'shuts off' during sleep (it remains highly active, especially in REM).
That deep sleep and dreaming are the same stage (vivid dreaming occurs mainly in REM, not deep NREM).
That dreams must have hidden symbolic meanings (AP uses activation-synthesis and consolidation, not Freud).
That sleep disorders reflect a character flaw rather than a medical/biological condition.

topics.title: Sensation I, Thresholds, Transduction & Vision

lessons.title: Sensation I, Thresholds, Transduction & Vision
lessons.overview: How the senses begin: sensation vs. perception, transduction, thresholds (absolute, JND, Weber's law), sensory adaptation and interaction, synesthesia, and the visual system, the eye, rods and cones, and the trichromatic and opponent-process theories of color.
objectives: Explain sensation, transduction, thresholds (absolute, JND, Weber's law), adaptation, and sensory interaction.
Explain how the eye transduces light and compare the trichromatic and opponent-process theories of color.
essentialQuestions: How does the body turn light, sound, and touch into something the brain can use?
Why don't you feel your clothes on your skin all day long?

source.title: Elements of Psychophysics (founding the study of thresholds)
source.author: Gustav Fechner

lessons.title: Sensation II: Hearing, the Chemical Senses, Touch, Pain & Body Position
lessons.overview: The senses beyond vision: hearing (pitch theories, localization, conduction vs. sensorineural deafness), the chemical senses (olfaction, gustation, the six tastes, supertasters), touch and the gate-control theory of pain (and phantom limb), and the vestibular and kinesthetic senses.
objectives: Explain how the auditory, chemical, touch, and pain sensory systems transduce stimuli.
Explain the vestibular and kinesthetic senses and the gate-control theory of pain.
essentialQuestions: How do your other senses: beyond sight, turn the world into signals?
Why can someone feel pain in a limb that is no longer there?

source.title: Pain Mechanisms: A New Theory (the gate-control theory)
source.author: Ronald Melzack & Patrick Wall

lessons.title: Reading the Research: Practicing the AAQ & EBQ
lessons.overview: A synthesis lesson that turns Unit 1 content into AP exam skill: recognizing research designs, judging ethics and generalizability, reading data, and practicing both free-response task types, the AAQ (parts A-F) and the EBQ (defensible claim with cited evidence).
objectives: Determine the research design used in a study and evaluate its ethics and generalizability.
Practice the AAQ (parts A-F) and the EBQ (defensible claim + cited evidence + psychological reasoning).
essentialQuestions: How do psychologists read a real study and judge what it can (and cannot) tell us?
How do you build a defensible, evidence-based argument the AP way?

source.title: Multivitamin supplementation improves memory in older adults (the AP-style AAQ source)
source.author: Brickman, Yeung, et al. (COSMOS-Web)

vocab.def: Converting a physical stimulus into neural signals the brain can interpret.
The minimum stimulus detectable at least 50% of the time.
The principle that the JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.
Reduced sensitivity to an unchanging, constant stimulus over time.
Rods detect shape/movement in low light; cones detect color and detail in bright light.
Two complementary theories explaining how we perceive color.
Pitch is set by sound wavelength; loudness by amplitude.
Hearing loss from damage to inner-ear hair cells or the auditory nerve.
Olfaction is smell (skips the thalamus); gustation is taste.
Idea that a spinal 'gate' can block or allow pain signals to the brain.
Feeling sensation or pain in a limb that has been amputated.
Vestibular = balance (inner ear); kinesthetic = body-part position and movement.
Design that manipulates a variable with random assignment; supports causal claims.
Design that measures a relationship between variables; cannot establish causation.
The exact, measurable way a study defines a variable.
The extent to which findings apply beyond the study's sample to a population.
A finding unlikely to be due to chance.
Participants' agreement to take part with knowledge of what's involved.

misconceptions: That the absolute threshold is a fixed point (it is the level detected 50% of the time).
That only one theory explains color vision (trichromatic and opponent-process both apply at different stages).
That taste alone produces flavor (smell-taste interaction is essential).
That pain happens only at the injury site (it is processed in both body and brain; phantom limb proves the brain's role).
That a correlation proves one variable causes the other.
That an EBQ claim can be supported without citing the specific source of the evidence.

units.title: Cognition
units.blurb: How the mind perceives, thinks, remembers, forgets, and is measured.

topics.title: Can You Trust Your Senses?, Perception, Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up

lessons.title: Can You Trust Your Senses?, Perception, Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up
lessons.overview: Launch of Cognition. Students learn perception as an active, expectation-driven process (top-down vs. bottom-up), Gestalt organization, and selective attention, anchored by the Simons & Chabris inattentional-blindness study.
objectives: Explain how internal factors (schemas, perceptual sets) and external factors (context, culture) influence perception.
Identify the research design of a classic attention study and apply its finding to a new scenario.
essentialQuestions: Can you always trust your senses?
How do internal expectations and external context change what we perceive?

source.title: “Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events”
source.author: Daniel Simons & Christopher Chabris

lessons.title: Seeing in 3-D, Depth Cues, Constancies & Perceptual Illusions
lessons.overview: Students explain how binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) and the five CED monocular cues build a 3-D world from flat retinal images, how perceptual constancies stabilize what we see, and how illusions arise when those normally useful shortcuts misfire.
objectives: Distinguish binocular (retinal disparity, convergence) from monocular depth cues.
Explain how perceptual constancies stabilize perception and how illusions arise.
essentialQuestions: How do two flat retinal images become a three-dimensional world?
When do the brain's depth shortcuts produce illusions?

source.title: Note on the monocular depth cues addressed by the AP Exam (CED Exclusion Statement)
source.author: College Board AP Psychology CED

lessons.title: Unit 2 Review, Thinking Like a Cognitive Scientist (AAQ & EBQ Practice)
lessons.overview: Unit 2 synthesis and free-response practice. Students connect perception, thinking, memory, and intelligence into one model of cognition, then walk through the 7-point AAQ (parts A to F) and 7-point EBQ (parts A/B/C) using Roediger & Karpicke (2006) as the practice article.
objectives: Synthesize perception, thinking, memory, and intelligence into a coherent model of cognition.
Apply the 7-point AAQ (A, F) and 7-point EBQ (A/B/C) free-response formats to cognition research.
essentialQuestions: How do perception, thinking, memory, and intelligence connect into one science of cognition?
How do you analyze a research article (AAQ) and argue from evidence (EBQ)?

source.title: “Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention” (AAQ practice article)
source.author: Henry Roediger & Jeffrey Karpicke

vocab.def: Perception that begins with raw sensory data and builds to a whole.
Perception guided by prior expectations, knowledge, and context.
A mental framework of prior knowledge that organizes and filters perception.
A readiness to perceive in a certain way based on expectations.
Closure, figure-ground, proximity, and similarity, how the brain organizes perception.
Failing to notice an environmental change due to inattention.
Binocular cue: the difference between the two retinal images; bigger difference = nearer.
Binocular cue: the inward turning of the eyes as an object approaches.
Depth cues available to one eye (relative size, clarity, texture gradient, linear perspective, interposition).
Gradual change from coarse to fine texture, signaling increasing distance.
Perceiving an object as stable in size, shape, or color despite changing images.
Perception of motion when an object is not actually moving.
Article Analysis Question: analyze ONE summarized peer-reviewed study across parts A to F (7 points).
Evidence-Based Question: propose a claim and support it with TWO cited sources plus reasoning (7 points).
A precise statement of how a variable is measured or manipulated in a study.
The extent to which a study's findings apply beyond its specific sample.
A clear, arguable position that can be supported with evidence.
Research evaluated by other experts before publication.

misconceptions: That perception is a faithful 'video recording' of reality rather than an active interpretation.
That we consciously perceive everything in our sensory field.
That depth perception requires two eyes (monocular cues alone provide substantial depth).
That the retinal image and the perceived object are the same size.
That the AAQ and EBQ are interchangeable (one analyzes a single study; the other argues from sources).
That an EBQ claim can stand without reasoning that links cited evidence to the claim via psychological concepts.

topics.title: Thinking & Concepts, Prototypes, Schemas & the Building Blocks of Thought

lessons.title: Thinking & Concepts, Prototypes, Schemas & the Building Blocks of Thought
lessons.overview: First of two thinking lessons: the building blocks of thought. Students explain concepts and prototypes, how schemas grow through assimilation and accommodation, and how executive functions and creativity (divergent vs. convergent thinking; functional fixedness) shape goal-directed thought.
objectives: Explain how concepts, prototypes, and schemas (assimilation/accommodation) structure thinking.
Describe executive functions and creativity, and explain how functional fixedness hinders divergent thinking.
essentialQuestions: What are the basic units the mind uses to think?
How do mental frameworks help us think efficiently, and quietly lock in bias?

source.title: “On the Internal Structure of Perceptual and Semantic Categories” (the prototype/best-example view)
source.author: Eleanor Rosch

lessons.title: Judgment, Heuristics & Decision-Making, Why Smart People Make Bad Choices
lessons.overview: Second of two thinking lessons: judgment and decision-making. Students contrast algorithms with heuristics, analyze the representativeness and availability heuristics, and identify decision biases (mental set, priming, framing, gambler's and sunk-cost fallacies), anchored by Tversky & Kahneman (1973).
objectives: Distinguish algorithms from heuristics and explain the representativeness and availability heuristics.
Identify common decision-making biases (mental set, priming, framing, gambler's/sunk-cost fallacies) in scenarios.
essentialQuestions: Why don't people always make good decisions?
How do mental shortcuts help us think fast, and lead us astray?

source.title: “Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability”
source.author: Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman

vocab.def: A mental grouping of similar objects, events, or ideas; the basis of thought.
The best or most typical example of a concept.
A mental framework that organizes and interprets information.
Fitting new info into a schema unchanged (assimilation) vs. changing the schema (accommodation).
Cognitive processes that plan, organize, and carry out goal-directed behavior.
Inability to see a novel use for an object; blocks creative problem-solving.
A step-by-step method that guarantees a solution but can be slow.
A fast mental shortcut that can lead to errors in judgment.
Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
Judging by similarity to a prototype/stereotype, ignoring base rates.
How the wording of a choice changes the decision made.
Continuing a losing course of action because of past investment.

misconceptions: That a category is defined by a strict checklist of features rather than organized around a best example (prototype).
That creativity is a fixed 'gift' rather than a way of thinking that can be practiced.
That heuristics are simply 'errors', they are usually adaptive, fast, and often correct.
That more deliberation always means a better decision.

topics.title: What Is Memory?, Explicit, Implicit & Models of the Mind

lessons.title: What Is Memory?, Explicit, Implicit & Models of the Mind
lessons.overview: Opens the memory sequence. Students differentiate explicit (episodic, semantic) from implicit (procedural, prospective) memory, learn LTP as a biological basis, and compare the multi-store, working-memory (Baddeley & Hitch), and levels-of-processing models.
objectives: Differentiate explicit (episodic, semantic) from implicit (procedural, prospective) memory.
Compare the multi-store, working-memory, and levels-of-processing models of memory.
essentialQuestions: How does the brain represent a learned skill differently from a remembered event?
What models help psychologists map how memory works?

source.title: “Working Memory” (the central executive and its subsystems)
source.author: Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch

vocab.def: Consciously known, 'declarable' memory (episodic and semantic).
Memory hard to verbalize, such as procedural skills.
Strengthening of synaptic connections with repeated activation; a biological basis of memory.
Memory as sensory → short-term → long-term stages.
Baddeley & Hitch: central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad.
Memory depends on depth of encoding: structural, phonemic, semantic.

misconceptions: That memory is a single unified system rather than multiple interacting types and stages.
That short-term memory is a passive container rather than an active workspace.

topics.title: Encoding Memories

lessons.title: Getting It In: Encoding, Chunking, Mnemonics & the Spacing Effect
lessons.overview: How information gets INTO memory. Students explain encoding strategies (chunking, mnemonics, hierarchies) and the ~7±2 capacity limit, contrast massed vs. distributed practice (the spacing effect), and apply the serial position effect and levels of processing, anchored by Miller (1956).
objectives: Explain encoding strategies (chunking, mnemonics, hierarchies) and the ~7±2 capacity limit.
Distinguish the spacing effect and serial position effect and apply them to studying.
essentialQuestions: What strategies actually get information into memory?
Why does spreading studying over time beat cramming?

source.title: “The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two”
source.author: George A. Miller

vocab.def: Getting information into memory through processing and strategy.
Grouping information into meaningful units to expand short-term capacity.
A memory aid, such as the method of loci, that organizes material.
Better long-term memory from study distributed over time than from cramming.
Better recall for items at the beginning and end of a list.
Encoding meaning; the deepest and most durable kind of encoding.

misconceptions: That cramming is as effective for long-term memory as spaced study.
That short-term memory capacity is unlimited.

topics.title: Holding On, Storing Memories, Rehearsal & Memory Systems

lessons.title: Holding On, Storing Memories, Rehearsal & Memory Systems
lessons.overview: How memory is held over time. Students compare sensory, short-term/working, and long-term memory by duration and capacity, distinguish maintenance from elaborative rehearsal, and describe amnesia (retrograde/anterograde) and Alzheimer's factually, anchored by Sperling (1960).
objectives: Compare sensory, short-term/working, and long-term memory by duration, capacity, and content.
Distinguish maintenance from elaborative rehearsal and retrograde from anterograde amnesia.
essentialQuestions: How long, and how much, can each memory system hold?
What happens to storage when the brain is injured or diseased?

source.title: “The Information Available in Brief Visual Presentations” (the partial-report study)
source.author: George Sperling

vocab.def: Brief (~0.5 s) visual sensory memory.
Brief (~3 to 4 s) auditory sensory memory.
Repetition that holds information in short-term memory.
Linking new information to meaning for stronger long-term storage.
Loss of memories formed before an injury or onset.
Inability to form new long-term memories after an injury or onset.

misconceptions: That sensory memory lasts more than a second or two.
That all amnesia means forgetting the past (anterograde blocks new learning instead).

topics.title: Retrieving Memories

lessons.title: Pulling It Back: Retrieval, Cues & the Power of Testing
lessons.overview: How memory comes back OUT. Students distinguish recall from recognition, explain context-, state-, and mood-dependent retrieval and encoding specificity, and apply the testing effect and metacognition to studying, anchored by Godden & Baddeley (1975).
objectives: Distinguish recall from recognition and explain context-, state-, and mood-dependent retrieval.
Explain the testing effect and metacognition and apply them to studying.
essentialQuestions: Why can a smell or a place suddenly bring back a flood of memories?
Why does testing yourself beat re-reading?

source.title: “Context-Dependent Memory in Two Natural Environments: On Land and Underwater”
source.author: Duncan Godden & Alan Baddeley

vocab.def: Retrieving information without cues (fill-in-the-blank).
Identifying information with cues (multiple choice).
A stimulus that helps trigger a stored memory.
Better retrieval in the same environment as encoding.
Easier recall of memories matching one's current mood.
Stronger memory from self-testing (retrieval) than from re-reading.

misconceptions: That re-reading is the most effective study method (retrieval practice is stronger).
That recognition and recall are equally difficult.

topics.title: Why Memory Fails, Forgetting, the Forgetting Curve & Interference

lessons.title: Why Memory Fails, Forgetting, the Forgetting Curve & Interference
lessons.overview: First of two forgetting lessons. Students explain the forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus), distinguish encoding failure from retrieval failure (tip-of-the-tongue), analyze proactive vs. retroactive interference, and evaluate repression as a contested psychodynamic claim.
objectives: Explain the forgetting curve and distinguish encoding failure from inadequate retrieval (tip-of-the-tongue).
Distinguish proactive from retroactive interference and evaluate repression as a contested claim.
essentialQuestions: Why do we forget so much, so fast?
How do competing memories crowd each other out?

source.title: “Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology” (the forgetting curve)
source.author: Hermann Ebbinghaus

lessons.title: The Misinformation Effect: How a Question Can Reshape a Memory (Loftus)
lessons.overview: Second of two forgetting lessons, centered on Loftus. Students explain reconstructive memory and the misinformation effect (Loftus & Palmer, 1974), distinguish source amnesia and imagination inflation, and apply the science to eyewitness reliability and wrongful conviction.
objectives: Explain reconstructive memory and the misinformation effect using the Loftus & Palmer study.
Distinguish source amnesia and imagination inflation and apply them to eyewitness reliability.
essentialQuestions: Why aren't our memories recorded exactly as we experienced them?
How can a single word in a question reshape what someone 'remembers'?

source.title: “Reconstruction of Automobile Destruction” (the verb-wording study)
source.author: Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer

vocab.def: Ebbinghaus's finding that forgetting is rapid at first, then levels off.
Forgetting because information never entered long-term memory.
Temporary inability to retrieve a word that is known to be stored.
Old information disrupting recall of new information.
New information disrupting recall of old information.
A contested psychodynamic claim that distressing memories are pushed from awareness.
Memory rebuilt at retrieval, filling gaps with assumptions.
Post-event misleading information distorting a memory.
Remembering information but misattributing its source.
Imagining an event raising false confidence that it occurred.
The process by which memories stabilize, and can be altered, over time.
A question whose wording can implant a detail into a memory.

misconceptions: That forgetting always means a memory is permanently erased (much is retrieval failure).
That repression is an established mechanism rather than a contested psychodynamic claim.
That memory is a permanent, accurate recording that can be 'played back.'
That confidence in a memory guarantees its accuracy.

topics.title: Intelligence and Achievement

lessons.title: Measuring the Mind: Intelligence, IQ & the Mindset That Shapes Achievement
lessons.overview: First of three intelligence lessons. Students explain the g-versus-multiple-abilities debate, how IQ was originally computed and is used today (honoring the CED exclusion), the achievement/aptitude distinction, and how fixed vs. growth mindset shapes achievement, anchored by Spearman (1904).
objectives: Explain the debate over general intelligence (g) versus multiple abilities and how IQ is computed.
Distinguish achievement from aptitude tests and explain how fixed vs. growth mindset affects achievement.
essentialQuestions: Is intelligence one general ability or many?
How is intelligence measured: and how does belief about it shape achievement?

source.title: “General Intelligence, Objectively Determined and Measured” (the case for g)
source.author: Charles Spearman

lessons.title: Psychometric Principles: What Makes a Test Trustworthy?
lessons.overview: Second of three intelligence lessons, focused on psychometrics. Students define standardization, validity (construct, predictive), and reliability (test-retest, split-half), and explain the crucial distinction that a test can be reliable without being valid, anchored by Anastasi & Urbina (1997).
objectives: Define standardization, validity (construct/predictive), and reliability (test-retest/split-half).
Explain why reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity, using a concrete example.
essentialQuestions: What makes a psychological test scientifically trustworthy?
How can a test be consistent yet still be measuring the wrong thing?

source.title: “Psychological Testing” (the requirements for a sound assessment)
source.author: Anne Anastasi & Susana Urbina

lessons.title: Fairness & the Mind, Flynn Effect, Stereotype Threat & Test Misuse
lessons.overview: Third of three intelligence lessons, on fairness and equity. Students explain the Flynn effect and why within-group variation exceeds between-group differences, analyze stereotype threat and lift, and confront the documented misuse of intelligence testing, anchored by Steele & Aronson (1995).
objectives: Explain the Flynn effect and why within-group variation exceeds between-group differences.
Explain stereotype threat, stereotype lift, and the historical misuse of intelligence testing, grounded in research.
essentialQuestions: If IQ scores have risen for decades, what does that say about nature vs. environment?
How have intelligence tests been used to expand, and to deny, opportunity?

A test predicting a person's future performance.
The belief that intelligence is unchangeable from birth.
The belief that intelligence is malleable through effort and experience.
Consistent test administration and scoring, interpreted against a comparison group.
Whether a test measures what it is designed to measure.
Whether a test truly captures the concept it claims to measure.
Whether a test successfully forecasts a future outcome.
Whether a test yields consistent results across administrations.
Consistency across retakes (test-retest) or between halves of a test (split-half).
The long-term rise in average IQ scores across much of the world.
Anxiety about confirming a negative stereotype that can lower performance.
A performance boost from awareness of a positive stereotype.
Differences among individuals inside a group (greater than between-group differences).
Average differences between groups, largely reflecting environment, not innate ability.
Using assessment scores to unfairly limit access to jobs, schooling, or immigration.

misconceptions: That IQ is a fixed, complete, or perfectly objective measure of a person's worth or potential.
That intelligence is fixed at birth and cannot change with environment or effort.
That a reliable test is automatically valid (consistency is not the same as accuracy).

That between-group score gaps reflect innate, fixed differences in ability.
That intelligence tests are neutral tools that have never been used to harm or exclude.

units.title: Development and Learning
units.blurb: How people change across a lifespan, and how experience teaches.

topics.title: Themes & Methods in Developmental Psychology

lessons.title: Themes & Methods in Developmental Psychology
lessons.overview: Launches Unit 3 with the enduring themes (stability/change, nature/nurture, continuous/discontinuous) and the two core developmental research designs (cross-sectional vs. longitudinal), per CED Topic 3.1.
objectives: Explain how the three enduring themes inform developmental psychology (3.1.A).
Describe how cross-sectional and longitudinal designs inform understanding of behavior, including their trade-offs (3.1.B).
essentialQuestions: What big questions guide how psychologists study change across the lifespan?
How do cross-sectional and longitudinal designs each reveal, and hide, different things about development?

source.title: Adaptation: How a Longitudinal Study Works (research-methods description)
source.author: AP Psychology CED, Topic 3.1.B

lessons.title: Unit 3 Review: Mastering the AAQ/EBQ
lessons.overview: Synthesizes Unit 3 and trains the two AP free-response tasks: the Article Analysis Question (AAQ, Parts A, F, F worth 2 pts) and the Evidence-Based Question (EBQ, Parts A, C), with a worked study description for practice.
objectives: Connect the unit’s developmental and learning concepts across themes and the lifespan.
Apply the AAQ and EBQ scoring criteria to earn full credit on AP free-response questions.
essentialQuestions: How do the unit’s developmental and learning concepts connect across the lifespan?
How do I earn every point on the AP Article Analysis Question (AAQ) and Evidence-Based Question (EBQ)?

That development stops once a person reaches adulthood.
That an EBQ point is earned by citing a source without explaining or applying a concept.
That an operational definition can be vague rather than measurable.

topics.title: Physical Development Across the Lifespan

lessons.title: Physical Development Across the Lifespan
lessons.overview: Traces physical development across the lifespan per CED Topic 3.2, prenatal teratogens, infant reflexes and the visual cliff, critical/sensitive periods and imprinting, pubertal milestones, and adult decline.
objectives: Explain how prenatal, infant, adolescent, and adult physical development apply to behavior and mental processes (3.2.A, D).
Interpret the visual-cliff study as evidence about early depth perception (3.2.B.3).
essentialQuestions: How do prenatal influences and infant reflexes shape the start of life?
What physical milestones mark adolescence and adulthood, and how does the body change as we age?

The period of sexual maturation when reproductive ability develops.

That physical development follows an identical clock in every child (order is similar; timing varies).

topics.title: Gender & Sexual Orientation in Development

lessons.title: Gender & Sexual Orientation in Development
lessons.overview: Distinguishes sex from gender and examines socialization and sexual orientation (CED Topic 3.3), with a focus on why these topics require non-experimental (correlational) designs (Skill 2.C). Handled factually, respectfully, and age-appropriately.
objectives: Describe how sex and gender influence socialization and other aspects of development (3.3.A).
Evaluate the appropriate use of research-design elements in non-experimental methodologies (Skill 2.C).
essentialQuestions: How do sex and gender differ, and how does each influence socialization and development?
Why must psychologists study sex, gender, and sexual orientation with NON-experimental designs?

source.title: On Studying Sex and Gender Without Experiments (research-methods description)
source.author: AP Psychology CED, Topic 3.3 / Skill 2.C

The behaviors, attitudes, and roles a culture associates with a given identity.
A person’s internal sense of their own gender.
The lifelong process of learning a society’s expected behaviors and roles.

An enduring pattern of emotional and sexual attraction to others.

misconceptions: That sex and gender are the same thing.
That a correlational study about gender can prove cause and effect.

topics.title: Cognitive Development: Piaget

lessons.title: Cognitive Development: Piaget
lessons.overview: First cognitive-development lesson (CED Topic 3.4): Piaget’s constructivist theory, schemas, assimilation/accommodation, and the four stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational) with their signature competencies and errors.
objectives: Explain Piaget’s theory of cognitive development and apply it to behavior (3.4.A.1).
Identify the signature competencies and errors of each Piagetian stage (3.4.A.1.i, iv).
essentialQuestions: How does Piaget say children actively BUILD knowledge rather than passively receive it?
What can: and can’t, a child do at each of Piaget’s four stages, and how do we test it?

source.title: The Psychology of the Child (on assimilation and accommodation)
source.author: Jean Piaget & Bärbel Inhelder

lessons.title: Cognitive Development: Vygotsky & Information-Processing
lessons.overview: Second cognitive-development lesson (CED Topic 3.4): Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory (ZPD, scaffolding, private speech), the information-processing view of cognitive growth, and cognition in late adulthood (crystallized vs. fluid intelligence, dementia).
objectives: Explain Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory and the information-processing view, and apply them to behavior (3.4.A.2 to 3).
Distinguish crystallized from fluid intelligence and describe cognitive change in adulthood (3.4.A.3).
essentialQuestions: How does Vygotsky’s social view of learning differ from Piaget’s solo “little scientist”?
How do information-processing skills sharpen in childhood, and how does cognition change in late adulthood?

source.title: Mind in Society (on the zone of proximal development)

Interpreting new information in terms of an existing schema.
Adjusting a schema to incorporate new information.
The understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight (sensorimotor stage).
The preoperational difficulty in taking another person’s point of view.
The principle that quantity stays the same despite changes in shape (gained in concrete operational stage).
The range between what a learner can do alone and with skilled help (Vygotsky).
Temporary, fading support that helps a learner do what they cannot yet do alone.
Children’s self-directed talk that guides behavior and is later internalized as thought.
A view of cognition as the input, storage, and retrieval of information, like a computer.
Accumulated knowledge and skills that remain stable or grow with age.
The ability to reason quickly about novel problems, which tends to decline with age.

That every adult reaches full formal operational thought (Piaget said not all do).
That Vygotsky and Piaget say the same thing (Vygotsky stresses social/cultural support; Piaget stresses the solo constructor).
That dementia is a normal, inevitable part of growing old (it is a disorder, not typical aging).

topics.title: Communication & Language Development

lessons.title: Communication & Language Development
lessons.overview: Covers the components of language (phonemes, morphemes, semantics, grammar/syntax), the universal stages of acquisition (gestures, cooing, babbling, one-word, telegraphic), and overgeneralization as evidence of rule-learning, per CED Topic 3.5.
objectives: Explain how key components of language and communication apply to behavior (3.5.A).
Explain how language develops in humans through universal stages and rule-based errors (3.5.B).
essentialQuestions: What are the building blocks that make human language a uniquely generative system?
What predictable stages do children pass through as they learn to speak, and why do their errors reveal rules?

source.title: Components and Stages of Language (research-methods description)

The smallest unit of language that carries meaning.

Applying a grammatical rule too broadly (e.g., “goed” for “went”).

That a grammatical error means a child is falling behind rather than applying a rule.

topics.title: Attachment & Parenting (Harlow, Ainsworth)

lessons.title: Attachment & Parenting (Harlow, Ainsworth)
lessons.overview: First of three social-emotional lessons (CED Topic 3.6): attachment and contact comfort (Harlow’s monkeys), attachment styles and separation anxiety (Ainsworth’s Strange Situation, temperament), and the three parenting styles with cultural variation.
objectives: Explain how attachment and parenting styles apply to social development (3.6.A.2 to 3).
Interpret Harlow’s and Ainsworth’s studies as evidence about attachment (3.6.A.3.ii).
essentialQuestions: How do early attachment bonds form, and what did Harlow’s and Ainsworth’s studies reveal?
How do the major parenting styles differ, and why do their effects vary across cultures?

source.title: The Nature of Love (presidential address, American Psychological Association)
source.author: Harry F. Harlow

lessons.title: Social Context: Bronfenbrenner, Family & Peers
lessons.overview: Second social-emotional lesson (CED Topic 3.6): Bronfenbrenner’s five ecological systems (micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono), the family and peer microsystems, parallel vs. pretend play, and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) with sociocultural variation.
objectives: Explain how Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems apply to social development (3.6.A.1).
Explain how family, peers, and play shape social development, and how ACEs affect the lifespan (3.6.A.4, A.7).
essentialQuestions: How does Bronfenbrenner show that a child develops inside nested layers of environment?
How do the family, peers, and play shape social development beyond the parent-child bond?

source.title: The Ecology of Human Development (on nested environmental systems)
source.author: Urie Bronfenbrenner

lessons.title: Social-Emotional Development: Erikson & Identity
lessons.overview: Third social-emotional lesson (CED Topic 3.6): Erikson’s eight psychosocial stages, adolescent identity statuses (achievement/diffusion/foreclosure/moratorium) and multiple identities, adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable), and adult social development (the social clock, emerging adulthood).
objectives: Explain Erikson’s psychosocial stages and how social development relates to behavior (3.6.A.6).
Explain adolescent identity formation, egocentrism, and adult social milestones (3.6.A.5, A.8).
essentialQuestions: How does Erikson say we grow by resolving a conflict at each stage of life?
How do adolescents form identity, and how does social development continue across adulthood?

The culturally preferred timing of life events such as marriage or retirement.

topics.title: Classical Conditioning (Pavlov, Little Albert)

lessons.title: Classical Conditioning (Pavlov, Little Albert)
lessons.overview: Introduces the behavioral perspective and classical conditioning (CED Topic 3.7): Pavlov’s UCS/UCR/CS/CR, acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization/discrimination, higher-order conditioning, conditioned emotion via Watson & Rayner’s Little Albert, Garcia & Koelling’s taste aversion, biological preparedness, and habituation.

Apply the Pavlovian terms and processes to novel scenarios, including conditioned emotion (3.7.A.1 to 5).

How can emotions themselves be conditioned, and what does Little Albert reveal about learned fear?
