misconceptions: That the CS and UCS are interchangeable labels (the UCS triggers a response unlearned; the CS only after pairing).
That extinction erases learning permanently (spontaneous recovery shows it does not).

topics.title: Operant Conditioning (Skinner, Schedules)

lessons.title: Operant Conditioning (Skinner, Schedules)
lessons.overview: Covers operant conditioning (CED Topic 3.8): Thorndike’s Law of Effect, Skinner’s chamber, the reinforcement/punishment matrix, primary vs. secondary reinforcers, shaping and instinctive drift, superstition and learned helplessness (Seligman & Maier), and continuous vs. the four partial reinforcement schedules.
objectives: Explain how operant conditioning applies to behavior and mental processes (3.8.A).
Differentiate reinforcement from punishment and identify the four partial schedules and their effects (3.8.A.2 to 5).
essentialQuestions: How do consequences: reinforcement and punishment, shape voluntary behavior?
Why does the SCHEDULE of reinforcement change how strong and lasting a behavior becomes?

source.title: Animal Intelligence (the Law of Effect, puzzle-box studies)
source.author: Edward L. Thorndike

vocab.def: Learning in which behavior is shaped by its consequences.
A consequence that increases the likelihood of a behavior.
Increasing a behavior by removing an unpleasant stimulus.
Reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior.
Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses; produces high, steady responding.
Passive resignation after learning one cannot control aversive events.

misconceptions: That negative reinforcement is the same as punishment (it increases behavior; punishment decreases it).
That continuous reinforcement makes behavior most resistant to extinction (partial, especially variable-ratio, does).

topics.title: Social, Cognitive & Biological Factors in Learning

lessons.title: Social, Cognitive & Biological Factors in Learning
lessons.overview: Closes the learning topics (CED Topic 3.9) with the social, cognitive, and biological factors reinforcement alone can’t explain: Bandura’s observational learning and vicarious conditioning (Bobo doll), Köhler’s insight learning, Tolman’s latent learning and cognitive maps, and biological preparedness/instinctive drift (Garcia & Koelling).
objectives: Explain how social learning applies to behavior and mental processes (3.9.A).
Explain how cognitive (insight, latent learning) and biological factors apply to learning (3.9.B).
essentialQuestions: How can we learn without any direct reward, by watching others, by insight, or by exploring?
What did Bandura, Köhler, and Tolman show about the social, cognitive, and biological limits of pure reinforcement?

source.title: Transmission of Aggression Through Imitation of Aggressive Models (the Bobo doll study)
source.author: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross & Sheila Ross

vocab.def: Learning by watching and imitating others.
Learning from the consequences experienced by others.
Sudden realization of a problem’s solution without trial-and-error.
Learning that occurs without reinforcement and is not shown until useful.
A mental representation of the layout of one’s environment.
An evolved predisposition to learn certain associations more easily than others.

misconceptions: That all learning requires direct reinforcement (observational, insight, and latent learning do not).
That biology places no limits on conditioning (preparedness and instinctive drift show it does).

units.title: Social Psychology and Personality
units.blurb: How other people shape us, and what makes a self consistent.

topics.title: Attribution Theory & Person Perception

lessons.title: Attribution Theory & Person Perception
lessons.overview: Opens Unit 4 with attribution theory (dispositional vs. situational; explanatory style), the three classic attribution biases (fundamental attribution error, actor/observer bias, self-serving bias) and locus of control, plus person perception (mere exposure effect, self-fulfilling prophecy, social comparison, relative deprivation), per CED Topic 4.1.
objectives: Explain how dispositional and situational attributions and attribution biases shape how we explain behavior (4.1.A).
Explain how mere exposure, self-fulfilling prophecy, and social comparison shape person perception (4.1.A).
essentialQuestions: When someone cuts you off in traffic, do you blame THEM or the SITUATION, and why does it matter?
How do mental shortcuts in how we explain and perceive others shape our behavior?

source.title: The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations (on perceiving causes)
source.author: Fritz Heider

vocab.def: Explaining behavior by an internal cause (personality, ability, effort).
Explaining behavior by an external cause (circumstances, environment).
Overweighting disposition and underweighting situation when judging others.
Crediting the self for successes but blaming the situation for failures.
Increased liking for a stimulus simply because it is encountered repeatedly.
A belief that leads to behavior that makes the belief come true.

misconceptions: That the fundamental attribution error means people never consider the situation, it means they UNDERWEIGHT it when judging others.
That the mere exposure effect requires liking the stimulus at first, repeated exposure alone increases liking.

topics.title: Attitude Formation, Change & Cognitive Dissonance

lessons.title: Attitude Formation, Change & Cognitive Dissonance
lessons.overview: Covers attitudes and attitude change: how attitudes form (explicit/implicit; attitude, behavior link), why beliefs resist change (belief perseverance, confirmation bias), cognitive dissonance and its reduction (Festinger; the $1/$20 study), and persuasion (the elaboration likelihood model's central/peripheral routes, halo effect, foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face), per CED Topic 4.2.
objectives: Explain how attitudes form and how belief perseverance and cognitive dissonance apply to attitude formation and change (4.2.B).
Distinguish central and peripheral routes to persuasion and identify common compliance techniques (4.2.B).
essentialQuestions: Why do people change their ATTITUDES to match their ACTIONS, instead of the other way around?
What makes an attitude stick: and what makes someone abandon a belief?

source.title: “Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance” (the $1 vs. $20 study)
source.author: Leon Festinger & James M. Carlsmith

lessons.title: Stereotypes, Prejudice & Bias
lessons.overview: Examines stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination: stereotypes and implicit attitudes producing prejudice/discrimination, biased views of groups (in-group bias, out-group homogeneity, ethnocentrism, just-world phenomenon), the social and cognitive roots of prejudice, and evidence-based ways to reduce it (cooperative contact, superordinate goals), per CED Topic 4.2 (stereotype/bias strand).
objectives: Explain how stereotypes and implicit attitudes contribute to prejudice and discrimination (4.2/4.2.A).
Identify in-group/out-group biases and explain evidence-based methods for reducing prejudice (4.3).
essentialQuestions: How do stereotypes and attitudes we may not even be aware of turn into prejudice and discrimination?
Why do we so easily see our own group as varied but other groups as “all the same”?

source.title: The Nature of Prejudice (on categorization and the in-group)
source.author: Gordon W. Allport

vocab.def: Feelings, beliefs, and behavioral tendencies toward a person, object, or idea.
Holding to a belief even after it has been discredited by evidence.
Seeking information that confirms one's existing beliefs.
Mental discomfort from a conflict between attitudes and actions.
Persuasion through a central (logic) or peripheral (cues) route.
Gaining a large compliance by first securing a small one.
A generalized belief about the members of a group.
A usually negative attitude toward a group and its members.
Negative behavior or action directed toward members of a group.
An attitude held outside conscious awareness that still influences behavior.
Seeing out-group members as more alike than they are.
The belief that people get the outcomes they deserve.

misconceptions: That cognitive dissonance is reduced by larger rewards, in fact, weaker external justification produces MORE attitude change.
That persuasion always works through logic, the peripheral route changes attitudes through surface cues like attractiveness.
That prejudice (attitude) and discrimination (behavior) are the same thing.
That only people who consciously dislike a group can discriminate, implicit attitudes can drive biased behavior in people who sincerely reject prejudice.

topics.title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity & Obedience

lessons.title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity & Obedience
lessons.overview: Examines how social situations shape behavior: social norms, normative vs. informational influence, Asch's conformity study, Milgram's obedience study, and the situational conditions (proximity of authority and victim, defiant peers, legitimacy) that strengthen or weaken obedience, per CED Topic 4.3 (social-situation strand).
objectives: Explain how social norms and normative/informational influence shape behavior (4.3.A).
Describe what Asch's and Milgram's research reveals about the conditions strengthening conformity and obedience (4.3.A).
essentialQuestions: Will people deny what their own eyes clearly see just to agree with a group?
How far will ordinary people go to obey an authority figure, even to harm a stranger?

source.title: “Behavioral Study of Obedience” (procedure and results)
source.author: Stanley Milgram

lessons.title: Group Dynamics: Groupthink & Polarization
lessons.overview: Explores how groups shape individuals, group polarization, groupthink (Janis) and its remedies, social loafing, social facilitation, deindividuation, false consensus, social traps, and the individualism/collectivism frame, per CED Topic 4.3 (group-dynamics strand).
objectives: Explain how being in a group affects behavior via polarization, groupthink, social loafing, social facilitation, and deindividuation (4.3.C).
Identify remedies that counter groupthink and reduce social loafing (4.3.C).
essentialQuestions: How does being in a group change how hard we work and how extreme our views become?
Why do smart, well-meaning groups sometimes make terrible decisions?

source.title: Victims of Groupthink (defining the concept)
source.author: Irving L. Janis

lessons.title: The Bystander Effect & Prosocial Behavior
lessons.overview: Examines prosocial behavior and helping, altruism, the social reciprocity and social responsibility norms, the Darley & Latané bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility, the steps to helping (notice/interpret/feel responsible), and the conditions that increase helping, per CED Topic 4.3 (prosocial strand).
objectives: Explain how prosocial behavior and the bystander effect operate (4.3.C).
Identify conditions and norms that increase or decrease helping behavior (4.3.C).
essentialQuestions: Why might a person be LESS likely to get help in a crowd than if only one bystander were present?
What pushes people to help others: sometimes at great cost to themselves?

source.title: “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility”
source.author: John M. Darley & Bibb Latané

vocab.def: Adjusting behavior or thinking to match a group standard.
Conforming to gain approval or avoid rejection.
Conforming because others are believed to have correct information.
Following the direct commands of an authority figure.
A society's expectation for how members should behave.
An actor secretly working for the experimenter in a study.
Strengthening of a group's prevailing views through discussion.
Faulty decision-making driven by a group's desire for harmony and consensus.
Reduced individual effort when working in a group.
Improved performance on easy tasks when others are present.
Loss of self-awareness and restraint in anonymous group situations.
Overestimating how much others share our beliefs and behaviors.
Voluntary behavior intended to benefit another person.
Selfless concern for the welfare of others.
The tendency to be less likely to help when other bystanders are present.
Reduced sense of personal responsibility to act when others are present.
The expectation that we help those who have helped us.
The expectation that we help those who need help.

misconceptions: That conformity and obedience are the same, conformity follows peers/norms; obedience follows an authority's command.
That only “weak” or “bad” people obeyed Milgram, the disturbing finding is that ordinary people did, because of the situation.
That group discussion moderates opinions, among like-minded members it usually makes them MORE extreme (polarization).
That social facilitation always improves performance, it helps easy/well-learned tasks but can impair difficult ones.
That a bigger crowd makes a victim safer, diffusion of responsibility often makes help LESS likely.
That helping is purely instinctive: whether people help depends heavily on the situation (number of bystanders, clarity of the emergency).

topics.title: Psychodynamic Theory of Personality

lessons.title: Psychodynamic Theory of Personality
lessons.overview: Introduces the psychodynamic theory of personality: unconscious drives, the ego's defense mechanisms (repression, denial, displacement, projection, rationalization, reaction formation, regression, sublimation), projective assessment (Rorschach, TAT), and the scientific critique, per CED Topic 4.4 (psychodynamic strand). Per CED exclusion, Freud's psychosexual stages are NOT taught.
objectives: Explain how the psychodynamic theory defines personality through unconscious processes (4.4.A).
Identify ego defense mechanisms, explain how projective tests attempt to assess personality, and state the scientific critique (4.4.A).
essentialQuestions: Can forces you are NOT aware of drive your personality and behavior?
How do the mind's “defense mechanisms” protect us from anxiety, and how would a psychologist try to reveal them?

source.title: New Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis (on the unconscious)
source.author: Sigmund Freud

lessons.title: Humanistic Theory of Personality
lessons.overview: Presents the humanistic theory of personality (Carl Rogers): unconditional positive regard and the self-actualizing tendency as primary motivators, plus self-concept and congruence, with the theory's strengths and criticisms, contrasted with the psychodynamic view, per CED Topic 4.4 (humanistic strand). Per CED exclusion, Maslow's hierarchy of needs is NOT taught as required content.
objectives: Explain how the humanistic theory defines personality through unconditional positive regard and the self-actualizing tendency (4.4.B).
Distinguish the humanistic view of personality from the psychodynamic view and state its main criticisms.
essentialQuestions: What does a person need from others in order to grow into their best self?
How does the humanistic view of personality differ from Freud's darker, conflict-driven picture?

source.title: On Becoming a Person (the growth-promoting climate)
source.author: Carl R. Rogers

vocab.def: View that unconscious processes drive personality and behavior.
Thoughts, wishes, and memories outside conscious awareness.
Unconscious strategies the ego uses to protect itself from anxiety.
Banishing anxiety-arousing thoughts or memories from awareness.
Attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to others.
An assessment using ambiguous stimuli to reveal unconscious thoughts.
Personality view emphasizing growth, free will, and human potential.
Complete, non-judgmental acceptance of another person.
The innate drive to fulfill one's potential.
All the beliefs and feelings one holds about oneself.
Standards a person feels they must meet to be accepted.
A close match between one's real self and ideal self.

misconceptions: That defense mechanisms are conscious choices, Freud held they operate UNCONSCIOUSLY.
That projective tests are highly reliable, they are widely criticized for weak reliability and validity.
That humanistic theory ignores struggle, it holds that acceptance, not conflict, best fosters growth.
That unconditional positive regard means approving of all behavior, it means valuing the PERSON, not endorsing every act.

topics.title: Social-Cognitive & Trait Theories of Personality

lessons.title: Social-Cognitive & Trait Theories of Personality
lessons.overview: Covers two scientific theories of personality: social-cognitive theory (Bandura's reciprocal determinism, self-efficacy, self-esteem, self-concept) and trait theory (enduring characteristics; the Big Five measured via factor analysis and self-report inventories), plus the person, situation debate, per CED Topic 4.5 (social-cognitive & trait strands).
objectives: Explain how social-cognitive theory defines personality through reciprocal determinism and self-concept (4.5.A).
Explain how trait theories define personality and how the Big Five is measured via factor analysis (4.5.A).
essentialQuestions: Do you shape your environment, or does it shape you, or both at once?
Can a whole personality be captured by just FIVE broad traits?

source.title: Social Foundations of Thought and Action (on reciprocal determinism)
source.author: Albert Bandura

vocab.def: View that personality arises from person, behavior, environment interaction.
Mutual influence among behavior, personal factors, and environment.
Belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task.
How one views oneself and one's relation to others.
An enduring characteristic that produces typical responses to stimuli.
Five broad personality dimensions: O, C, E, A, and emotional stability.

misconceptions: That self-efficacy and self-esteem are identical, self-efficacy is task-specific belief; self-esteem is overall self-worth.
That the Big Five are types you fall into, they are continuous DIMENSIONS on which everyone scores high or low.

topics.title: Theories of Motivation: Drives, Arousal, Incentives

lessons.title: Theories of Motivation: Drives, Arousal, Incentives
lessons.overview: Surveys theories of motivation: drive-reduction (homeostasis), arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law, sensation seeking, self-determination theory (intrinsic vs. extrinsic), incentive theory, the overjustification effect, and Lewin's three motivational conflicts, per CED Topic 4.6 (motivation-theory strand).
objectives: Explain how drive-reduction, arousal, self-determination, incentive, and sensation-seeking theories account for motivation (4.6.A).
Explain the overjustification effect and identify Lewin's three types of motivational conflict (4.6.A).
essentialQuestions: Are we pushed by internal needs, or pulled by outside rewards, and is there a “just right” level of arousal?
Can paying someone to do something they already love actually KILL their motivation?

source.title: “The Relation of Strength of Stimulus to Rapidity of Habit-Formation”
source.author: Robert M. Yerkes & John D. Dodson

lessons.title: Hunger, Belonging & Social Motivation
lessons.overview: Examines hunger as a complex motivated behavior, the hypothalamus, the hunger/satiety hormones ghrelin and leptin, and external eating cues, and the fundamental human need to belong and affiliate, per CED Topic 4.6 (eating & belongingness strand).
objectives: Explain how hormones (ghrelin, leptin) and external factors regulate eating (4.6.B).
Explain how belongingness and affiliation motivate behavior and mental processes (4.6.B).
essentialQuestions: What makes you feel hungry or full: and why isn't it only about an empty stomach?
How powerful is the human need to belong as a motivator of behavior?

source.title: “The Need to Belong” (on belonging as a fundamental motivation)
source.author: Roy F. Baumeister & Mark R. Leary

vocab.def: The needs and desires that energize and direct behavior.
Theory that needs create drives we act to reduce, restoring homeostasis.
Performance is best at a moderate (not too low, not too high) level of arousal.
Doing an activity for its own sake, out of interest or enjoyment.
Doing an activity for an external reward or to avoid punishment.
When an external reward reduces intrinsic motivation for an already-enjoyed activity.
Brain region that regulates hunger, satiety, and other basic drives.
Hunger-stimulating hormone secreted by an empty stomach.
Satiety hormone secreted by fat cells that decreases appetite.
The feeling of fullness that ends eating.
The fundamental human need to form lasting, positive relationships.
The desire to associate with and seek the company of others.

misconceptions: That more arousal always improves performance, the Yerkes-Dodson law shows an inverted-U, with an optimal middle.
That extrinsic rewards always boost motivation, the overjustification effect shows they can undermine intrinsic motivation for already-enjoyed tasks.
That hunger is controlled only by the stomach, the hypothalamus and hormones, plus external cues, all play roles.
That ghrelin and leptin do the same job, ghrelin raises appetite, leptin signals fullness.

topics.title: Theories of Emotion

lessons.title: Theories of Emotion
lessons.overview: Introduces emotion as a physiological-plus-cognitive process and the historical debate over the order of those components (succession, simultaneity, cognitive label required), plus the facial-feedback hypothesis (mixed evidence) and Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory, per CED Topic 4.7 (emotion-theory strand). Per CED exclusion, specific emotion-theory NAMES are not required.
objectives: Explain how theories of emotion describe the relationship between physiological arousal and cognition (4.7.A).
Explain the facial-feedback hypothesis and the broaden-and-build theory (4.7.A).
essentialQuestions: When you feel fear, does your racing heart come BEFORE the feeling, or does the feeling cause the racing heart, or both at once?
Can the act of smiling actually make you feel happier?

source.title: “The Broaden-and-Build Theory of Positive Emotions”
source.author: Barbara L. Fredrickson

lessons.title: Emotion, Culture & Display Rules
lessons.overview: Covers the universality debate (six possibly-common emotions; mixed results), cultural display rules and elicitors (varying by gender, age, class), how culture shapes both expressing and reading emotion, and cross-cultural competence, per CED Topic 4.7 (cultural-expression strand).
objectives: Explain how social norms and experiences influence emotional expression, including display rules and elicitors (4.7.B).
Evaluate the evidence on the universality of emotional expression across cultures (4.7.B).
essentialQuestions: Do people everywhere show happiness, fear, and anger the same way, or does culture rewrite the rules?
How do cultural “display rules” govern when and how we are allowed to show what we feel?

source.title: Cross-cultural research on emotional display rules (CED-aligned summary)
source.author: AP Psychology CED, Topic 4.7

lessons.title: Unit 4 Review (AAQ/EBQ)
lessons.overview: Closes Unit 4 with a synthesis of the four threads (social psychology, personality, motivation, emotion) and an explicit, point-by-point walkthrough of the 7-point Article Analysis Question (parts A to F) and the 7-point Evidence-Based Question (claim + cited, applied evidence), plus point-maximizing strategy, in preparation for the unit assessment.
objectives: Synthesize the unit's key concepts across social psychology, personality, motivation, and emotion.
Explain how each point on the AAQ and EBQ is earned and apply point-maximizing strategies.
essentialQuestions: How do the four big threads of Unit 4, social psychology, personality, motivation, and emotion, fit together?
How do you earn every point on the AAQ and the EBQ?

source.title: Released free-response scoring guidance (how AAQ/EBQ points are awarded)
source.author: AP Psychology CED, Section II task models

vocab.def: A response involving physiological arousal, expressive behavior, and conscious experience.
The bodily arousal (e.g., heart rate) involved in emotion.
The interpretation of arousal that defines which emotion is felt.
The idea that facial expressions influence emotional experience.
Theory that positive emotions broaden awareness and build resources.
Another term for emotion or feeling.
Cultural norms governing when and how emotions may be expressed.
Events or cues a culture treats as appropriate triggers for an emotion.
The degree to which emotional expressions are shared across cultures.
Shared norms, behaviors, and ideas transmitted across a group and generations.
The outward display (face, voice, posture) of an emotion.
A 7-point FRQ analyzing the design and findings of one study (parts A to F).
A 7-point FRQ building a cited argument from three peer-reviewed sources.
A precise statement of how a variable is measured in a study.
The extent to which results extend beyond the studied sample.
A specific, arguable thesis that the sources can support.
Connecting evidence to a psychological concept, theory, or finding to explain it.

misconceptions: That one emotion theory has been proven correct, the CED stresses the DISTINCTIONS (succession vs. simultaneity vs. label), not a winner.
That facial feedback is settled science, research has produced mixed results.
That all emotions are expressed identically worldwide, universality research shows mixed, partial agreement.
That display rules are universal: they vary by culture and even by group (gender, age, class) within a culture.
That citing a source is enough on the EBQ, the application point requires explaining how the evidence connects to a concept.
That an AAQ operational definition is a textbook definition, it must state how the variable was measured in THAT study.

units.title: Mental and Physical Health
units.blurb: Stress, wellbeing, disorders, and the treatments that help.

topics.title: Introduction to Health Psychology

lessons.title: Health Psychology & the Stress Response
lessons.overview: Launch of Unit 5 health psychology. Students learn the mind-body link, distinguish eustress/distress and traumatic stressors/daily hassles/ACEs, master Selye's three-stage general adaptation syndrome, and see why chronic stress harms physical health.
objectives: Explain how health psychology addresses physical health and wellness (CED 5.1.A-B).
Describe Selye's general adaptation syndrome and identify the stage of greatest illness susceptibility (CED 5.1.C).
essentialQuestions: How does stress affect the body and behavior, and when does it help versus harm?
What does the general adaptation syndrome reveal about why chronic stress makes us sick?

source.title: The Stress of Life (on the general adaptation syndrome)
source.author: Hans Selye

lessons.title: Unit 5 Synthesis & Course Wrap
lessons.overview: Unit 5 synthesis and course wrap. Students map the unit's through-line (health → defining → categories → treatment), match disorders to treatments, and practice the redesigned AP free-response tasks (AAQ parts A to F; EBQ defensible claim + cited sources), anchored by Smith & Glass's real meta-analysis and a researcher mega-card.
objectives: Integrate health psychology, classification, disorder categories, and treatments into one coherent framework (CED 5.1 to 5.5).
Apply the AAQ and EBQ rubrics to construct high-scoring free-response answers (AP Science Practices).
essentialQuestions: How do health, classification, the disorder categories, and treatments fit into one coherent picture?
How do you write a high-scoring AAQ and EBQ on the redesigned AP exam?

source.title: Putting it together, psychotherapy works (a real meta-analysis)
source.author: Mary Lee Smith & Gene V. Glass

vocab.def: Field studying how biological, psychological, and social factors affect physical health and illness.
The process of perceiving and responding to events appraised as threatening or challenging.
Stress appraised as motivating or beneficial.
Stress appraised as harmful or debilitating.
Selye's three-stage stress response: alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
Early-life stressors that can affect health and behavior across the lifespan.
Article Analysis Question: one source + parts A to F on the 7-point rubric.
Evidence-Based Question: three sources + parts A to C, requiring source citations.
A precise statement of how a variable is measured in a study.
The extent to which findings apply beyond the studied sample.
A clear, arguable thesis grounded in psychological science (EBQ part A).
Combining therapies and addressing biological, psychological, and social factors.

misconceptions: That all stress is bad: eustress can be motivating and adaptive.
That stress only affects mood, not physical health (it suppresses immunity and raises blood pressure).
That each disorder has exactly one 'correct' treatment (most are treated eclectically, often combining therapy and biomedical methods).
That the AAQ and EBQ are interchangeable (the AAQ analyzes one source; the EBQ argues a claim from three cited sources).

topics.title: Topics 5.1 to 5.2, Coping & Positive Psychology

lessons.title: Coping With Stress & Positive Psychology
lessons.overview: Coping and positive psychology. Students contrast problem- vs. emotion-focused coping, learn Taylor's tend-and-befriend, and survey positive psychology (gratitude, signature strengths, posttraumatic growth, subjective well-being, resilience).
objectives: Distinguish problem-focused and emotion-focused coping and explain tend-and-befriend (CED 5.1.C.2, 5.1.D).
Explain how positive psychology studies well-being via gratitude, strengths, and posttraumatic growth (CED 5.2).
essentialQuestions: What is the difference between solving a stressor and managing your reaction to it?
What does positive psychology say actually builds well-being, resilience, and happiness?

source.title: Positive Psychology: An Introduction (American Psychologist)
source.author: Martin E. P. Seligman & Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi

vocab.def: Reducing stress by working to solve or remove the stressor itself.
Reducing stress by managing one's emotional reactions to it.
Responding to stress by nurturing others and seeking social connection.
The study of factors that build well-being, resilience, and positive emotion.
A person's core character strengths/virtues; using them raises well-being.
Positive psychological change that can follow struggle with trauma or stress.

misconceptions: That emotion-focused coping is always inferior, it is adaptive when the stressor cannot be changed.
That positive psychology is just 'thinking happy thoughts' rather than an evidence-based research field.

topics.title: Explaining & Classifying Disorders

lessons.title: Defining & Classifying Psychological Disorders
lessons.overview: Defining and classifying disorders. Students apply dysfunction/distress/deviance, learn the DSM and ICD, weigh the costs and benefits of labels, and analyze Rosenhan's classic labeling study together with its later critique.
objectives: Describe the dysfunction/distress/deviance approaches to defining disorders (CED 5.3.A.1).
Explain the role of the DSM and ICD and the consequences (positive and negative) of diagnostic labeling (CED 5.3.A.2-3).
essentialQuestions: Where is the line between unusual behavior and a psychological disorder?
Why can a diagnosis both help a person AND harm them?

source.title: On Being Sane in Insane Places (Science)
source.author: David L. Rosenhan

lessons.title: Perspectives & the Biopsychosocial Model
lessons.overview: Explaining disorders. Students survey all seven perspectives on the causes of disorders, then integrate them with the biopsychosocial and diathesis-stress interaction models, using identical-twin discordance as the key application.
objectives: Explain how each of the seven psychological perspectives defines the causes of disorders (CED 5.3.B).
Apply the biopsychosocial and diathesis-stress interaction models (CED 5.3.C).
essentialQuestions: How do the seven psychological perspectives each explain WHY a disorder develops?
Why do most psychologists combine perspectives using the biopsychosocial and diathesis-stress models?

source.title: The Need for a New Medical Model (Science)
source.author: George L. Engel

vocab.def: Interference with everyday functioning; one criterion for a disorder.
Marked departure from cultural/social norms; one criterion for a disorder.
American Psychiatric Association's manual classifying mental disorders.
World Health Organization's classification of diseases/mental disorders.
Negative stereotyping and devaluing of people with disorders.
Using more than one psychological perspective in diagnosis/treatment.
Explains disorders as maladaptive learned associations.
Explains disorders as maladaptive thoughts and beliefs.
Explains disorders via maladaptive social/cultural dynamics.
Disorders arise from combined biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors.
Disorders emerge when genetic vulnerability meets life stress.
A predisposition or vulnerability (often genetic) to a disorder.

misconceptions: That deviation from norms ALONE defines a disorder (all three D's and context matter).
That a diagnostic label is purely objective and harmless, labels carry stigma and can bias perception.
That a disorder has a single cause from one perspective (most involve multiple interacting factors).
That a genetic vulnerability guarantees a disorder (diathesis-stress shows stress must also be present).

topics.title: Categories of Disorders

lessons.title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders
lessons.overview: First disorders lesson, one family per day. Students learn the neurodevelopmental category (onset in development, age-appropriateness), the two in-scope disorders, ADHD and autism spectrum disorder, and their environmental/physiological/genetic causes.
objectives: Explain what defines a neurodevelopmental disorder and its emphasis on age-appropriateness (CED 5.4.A.1).
Describe the symptoms of ADHD and ASD and their possible causes (CED 5.4.A.1-2).
essentialQuestions: What makes a disorder 'neurodevelopmental,' and how is it tied to age and maturity?
How do ADHD and autism spectrum disorder differ in their core symptoms?

source.title: Clinical vignette for analysis (fictional, NOT a real patient)
source.author: AP Psychology classroom case (composite)

lessons.title: Schizophrenic Spectrum Disorders
lessons.overview: The schizophrenic spectrum, one family per day. Students learn the five symptom areas, distinguish positive (added) from negative (absent) symptoms, including delusions vs. hallucinations and catatonia, and the in-scope causes: the dopamine hypothesis, genetic links, and prenatal virus exposure.
objectives: Identify the five symptom areas of the schizophrenic spectrum and distinguish positive vs. negative symptoms (CED 5.4.B.1).
Explain the dopamine hypothesis and other in-scope causes of schizophrenia (CED 5.4.B.2).
essentialQuestions: What are the five symptom areas of the schizophrenic spectrum?
How do positive and negative symptoms differ, and what may cause them?

lessons.title: Depressive & Bipolar Disorders
lessons.overview: The mood spectrum, one family per day. Students distinguish depressive disorders (MDD, persistent depressive) from bipolar disorders, learn mania vs. hypomania and Bipolar I vs. II, and survey the biopsychosocial causes.
objectives: Describe symptoms and possible causes of depressive disorders (CED 5.4.C).
Distinguish bipolar disorders (Bipolar I vs. II; cycling, mania, hypomania) and their causes (CED 5.4.D).
essentialQuestions: What distinguishes a depressive disorder from ordinary sadness?
How do bipolar disorders differ from depressive disorders, and from each other?

source.title: Darkness Visible: A Memoir of Madness

lessons.title: Anxiety Disorders
lessons.overview: Anxiety disorders, one family per day. Students learn what anxiety disorders share and distinguish the five in-scope disorders, specific phobia, agoraphobia (on its own), panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and GAD, plus culture-bound examples and the role of avoidance.
objectives: Distinguish the major anxiety disorders, including agoraphobia as its own disorder (CED 5.4.E.1).
Explain possible causes of anxiety disorders and how avoidance maintains them (CED 5.4.E.2).
essentialQuestions: What distinguishes the major anxiety disorders from one another?
How do specific phobia, agoraphobia, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and GAD differ?

lessons.title: Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders
lessons.overview: OCD and related disorders, one family per day. Students learn the obsession-compulsion cycle (with negative reinforcement), distinguish OCD from hoarding disorder and body dysmorphic disorder, and survey the biopsychosocial causes.
objectives: Define obsessions and compulsions and explain the cycle that maintains OCD (CED 5.4.F.1).
Distinguish OCD, hoarding disorder, and body dysmorphic disorder and their possible causes (CED 5.4.F.1-2).
essentialQuestions: How do obsessions and compulsions feed each other in a cycle?
What links OCD, hoarding disorder, and body dysmorphic disorder as a family?

lessons.title: Dissociative & Trauma-Related Disorders
lessons.overview: Dissociative and trauma-related disorders, one family per day. Students learn PTSD's intrusion/avoidance/arousal symptoms, the dissociative disorders (amnesia, fugue, DID), and the DID controversy taught honestly (posttraumatic model vs. Loftus's sociocognitive concerns).
objectives: Describe PTSD and the dissociative disorders, including dissociative amnesia and DID (CED 5.4.G.1, 5.4.H.1).
Explain both sides of the DID controversy and the biopsychosocial causes of these disorders (CED 5.4.G.2, 5.4.H.2; Science Practice 2).
essentialQuestions: How can the mind respond to overwhelming trauma by disconnecting from memory or identity?
Why is dissociative identity disorder one of psychology's most debated diagnoses?

lessons.title: Feeding & Eating Disorders
lessons.overview: Feeding and eating disorders, one family per day. Students distinguish anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder by their core behaviors, note distorted body image and medical risk, and survey the biopsychosocial causes, with a NEDA sensitivity strip.
objectives: Distinguish anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder (CED 5.4.I.1).
Explain the biological, psychological, and sociocultural causes of eating disorders (CED 5.4.I.2).
essentialQuestions: How do anorexia, bulimia, and binge-eating disorder differ in their core behaviors?
Why are eating disorders best understood through biological, psychological, AND sociocultural factors?

lessons.title: Personality Disorders
lessons.overview: Personality disorders, one family per day. Students learn what defines a personality disorder (enduring, inflexible, pervasive), the three clusters (A odd/eccentric, B dramatic/erratic, C anxious/fearful) with borderline and antisocial highlighted, and the biopsychosocial causes.
objectives: Explain what defines a personality disorder and the three-cluster organization (CED 5.4.J.1).
Describe borderline and antisocial personality disorders and the possible causes (CED 5.4.J.1-2).
essentialQuestions: What makes a pattern of personality a 'disorder' rather than just a personality style?
How do the three clusters (A, B, C) organize the personality disorders?

vocab.def: Disorders with onset in the developmental period (e.g., ADHD, ASD).
Early life, when neurodevelopmental disorders first appear.
Persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity beyond age-typical levels.
Persistent differences in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviors.
A range of presentations, strengths, and support needs across individuals.
Whether behavior fits a person's age and maturity, key to neurodevelopmental diagnosis.
Disorders marked by issues in one or more of five symptom areas.
False beliefs; a positive symptom of schizophrenia.
False perceptions; a positive symptom of schizophrenia.
Disorganized speech stringing words together nonsensically.
Greatly reduced emotional expression; a negative symptom.
Theory linking schizophrenia to excess dopamine activity.
Severe depressive episode impairing functioning for 2+ weeks.
Chronic, lower-grade depressed mood lasting years.
Period of abnormally elevated mood, energy, and activity in bipolar disorder.
Alternation between manic (or hypomanic) and depressive periods.
Bipolar disorder defined by full manic episodes.
Bipolar disorder with hypomania plus major depressive episodes.
Disorders marked by excessive fear/anxiety with behavioral disturbances.
Marked fear/anxiety toward a particular object or situation.
Intense fear of situations that are hard to escape or where help is unavailable.
Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks of overwhelming fear.
Intense fear of being judged or watched in social situations.
Prolonged, nonspecific anxiety not tied to one trigger.
Repetitive, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that cause anxiety.
Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce obsession-driven anxiety.
Disorder marked by obsessions and/or compulsions that impair functioning.
Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their actual value.
Preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws not observable to others.
Relief from anxiety after a compulsion, which strengthens the compulsion.
Disturbing reactions (intrusion, avoidance, arousal) following a traumatic event.
Disorders involving disruption of memory, identity, consciousness, or perception.
Inability to recall important personal information, usually after trauma or stress.
Subtype of dissociative amnesia with sudden travel or wandering plus amnesia.
Presence of two or more distinct identity states with memory gaps.
Two competing explanations of how DID develops (trauma-driven vs. suggestion-shaped).
Disorders involving persistent disturbances of eating that harm health or functioning.
Food restriction leading to low body weight with intense fear of weight gain.
Binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors (purging or non-purging).
Recurrent binge eating without regular compensatory behaviors.
Eating a large amount of food in a short time with a sense of loss of control.
Actions (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, excessive exercise) used to prevent weight gain.
Enduring, inflexible, pervasive pattern that deviates from norms and causes impairment.
Odd/eccentric personality disorders (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal).
Dramatic/erratic personality disorders (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic).
Anxious/fearful personality disorders (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive).
Pervasive disregard for and violation of others' rights, with lack of remorse.
Instability in relationships, self-image, and emotion, with impulsivity.

misconceptions: That any active or inattentive child 'has ADHD' (it requires a persistent, impairing, age-inappropriate pattern).
That vaccines cause autism (this is debunked; CED-listed causes are environmental, physiological, or genetic).
That 'positive symptom' means a good or helpful symptom (it means an added experience).
That schizophrenia means 'split personality' (that confuses it with dissociative identity disorder).
That 'bipolar' means rapid mood swings within a day (it refers to sustained manic/hypomanic and depressive periods).
That depression is just ordinary sadness rather than a sustained, impairing disorder.
That agoraphobia is the same as generalized anxiety (it is fear of escape-difficult SITUATIONS, a distinct disorder).
That a phobia is just ordinary fear (it is excessive, impairing fear of a specific object/situation).
That 'being OCD' means being tidy or organized (OCD involves distressing obsessions and impairing compulsions).
That insight ('I know it's irrational') stops the behavior (the compulsion is maintained by anxiety relief).
That DID is the same as schizophrenia ('split personality' vs. 'split from reality', different categories).
That the DID debate means DID is 'fake' (it is a recognized diagnosis whose CAUSES are debated).
That eating disorders are a 'choice' or simply extreme dieting (they are serious, high-mortality illnesses).
That a person must be visibly underweight to have an eating disorder (bulimia and BED often occur at normal weight).
That a personality disorder is just a strong personality 'style' (it is rigid, pervasive, and impairing).
That obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is the same as OCD (OCPD is a personality pattern of control/perfectionism, not obsessions/compulsions).

topics.title: Treatment of Disorders

lessons.title: Treating Disorders: Ethics, Psychodynamic & Humanistic Therapies
lessons.overview: Treatment, part 1. Students learn the ethics of treatment and the deinstitutionalization controversy, what psychotherapy and the eclectic approach are, and the goals/techniques of psychodynamic therapy (insight, free association, transference) and humanistic person-centered therapy (unconditional positive regard, empathy).
objectives: Explain the ethical principles of treatment and the deinstitutionalization controversy (CED 5.5.A).
Compare psychodynamic and humanistic therapies in goal and technique (CED 5.5).
essentialQuestions: What ethical principles must guide psychological treatment?
How do psychodynamic and humanistic therapies try to heal, and how do they differ?

source.title: On Becoming a Person (the conditions for growth)
source.author: Carl R. Rogers

lessons.title: Cognitive & Behavioral Therapies
lessons.overview: Treatment, part 2. Students learn cognitive therapies (Beck's cognitive triad/restructuring; Ellis's REBT and ABC model), CBT (and DBT for borderline), and behavioral therapies (Wolpe's systematic desensitization, exposure, aversion, and the operant token economy).
objectives: Explain cognitive therapies (Beck, Ellis) and CBT and how changing thoughts changes disorders (CED 5.5).
Explain behavioral therapies: systematic desensitization, exposure, and token economies, using learning principles (CED 5.5).
essentialQuestions: How do cognitive therapies change disorders by changing thoughts?
How do behavioral therapies use learning principles to change disorders?

source.title: Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy (the ABC of irrational beliefs)
source.author: Albert Ellis

lessons.title: Biological & Biomedical Treatments
lessons.overview: Treatment, part 3 (biomedical). Students learn psychopharmacology and the main drug classes (antidepressants/SSRIs, anti-anxiety/GABA, antipsychotics/dopamine, mood stabilizers/lithium), plus ECT, TMS, and psychosurgery, with the lobotomy as an ethics cautionary tale.
objectives: Identify the major biomedical drug classes and the disorders/neurotransmitters they target (CED 5.5).
Explain ECT, TMS, and psychosurgery, including their uses and ethical/historical cautions (CED 5.5).
essentialQuestions: How do biomedical treatments change the brain and body to treat disorders?
When are drugs, brain stimulation, or surgery used, and what are their limits?

source.author: U.S. National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

vocab.def: Treatment using psychological techniques via a therapist-client relationship.
Combining techniques from multiple therapeutic approaches to fit the client.
Therapy bringing unconscious conflicts into awareness for insight.
Client redirecting feelings about important people onto the therapist.
Rogers's humanistic therapy providing a supportive growth climate.
Total, nonjudgmental acceptance of a client by the therapist.
Treatment that changes maladaptive thoughts, beliefs, and attitudes.
Negative views of self, world, and future that sustain depression.
Ellis's therapy disputing irrational beliefs (ABC model).
Therapy combining cognitive restructuring with behavioral change.
Wolpe's exposure-plus-relaxation treatment up a fear hierarchy.
Operant therapy reinforcing desired behavior with tokens exchangeable for rewards.
Treating disorders by directly changing the brain or body (drugs, stimulation, surgery).
The study of how drugs affect mind and behavior.
Drugs that treat psychosis, often by dampening dopamine activity.
Drug treating bipolar disorder by reducing manic and depressive swings.
Controlled electrical seizure used for severe, treatment-resistant depression.
Rare, last-resort surgery altering brain tissue to change behavior (e.g., the discredited lobotomy).

misconceptions: That therapy is just 'giving advice' (psychotherapy uses structured psychological techniques within an ethical relationship).
That deinstitutionalization was a simple success (it improved dignity for many but left others without adequate community care).
That cognitive and behavioral therapies are the same (cognitive targets thoughts; behavioral targets learned behavior; CBT combines both).
That systematic desensitization just 'forces' someone to face a fear (it pairs graded exposure with relaxation up a hierarchy).
That medication 'cures' disorders by itself (drugs manage symptoms and often work best with therapy).
That ECT is the brutal procedure of old films (modern ECT is anesthetized, controlled, and used for severe, treatment-resistant cases).

units.title: AP Exam Review
units.blurb: Pulling five units back together before exam day.

topics.title: AP Exam Review: Units 0 & 1 (Research Methods · Biological Bases of Behavior)

lessons.title: Unit 0 to 1 Review: Research Methods & Biological Bases
lessons.overview: Cumulative recap of Unit 0 (methods, statistics, ethics) and Unit 1 (heredity/evolution, the neuron and action potential, neurotransmitters/hormones/drugs, the brain, sleep, and sensation), with a split-brain practice study and three balanced MCQs.
objectives: Match research questions to methods and distinguish random assignment from random sampling.
Trace a signal from neuron to brain and recap localization, sleep stages, and sensation thresholds using real studies (Sperry & Gazzaniga, Broca, Wernicke, Aserinsky & Kleitman).
essentialQuestions: Which research method answers which question, and what does each license you to claim?
How does a signal travel from a single neuron up to the whole brain, and how do sleep and sensation fit in?

source.title: Cerebral Organization and Behavior (split-brain research, paraphrased)
source.author: Roger W. Sperry

lessons.title: Unit 2 Review: Cognition
lessons.overview: Recap of Unit 2 Cognition: perception (top-down/bottom-up, attention), the memory pipeline (encoding/storage/retrieval/forgetting with Sperling, Miller, Baddeley, Ebbinghaus, Loftus), thinking and heuristics (Tversky & Kahneman, Rosch), and intelligence (Spearman, Flynn, Steele & Aronson), with the Loftus & Palmer practice study.
objectives: Trace information through the memory system and identify where and why forgetting occurs.
Apply heuristics and biases to scenarios and recap the principles of intelligence testing using real research.
essentialQuestions: How does information move through the memory system, and where does it break down?
Which shortcuts (heuristics) speed up thinking but bias it, and how do psychologists measure intelligence?

source.title: Reconstruction of Automobile Destruction (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Elizabeth F. Loftus & John C. Palmer

lessons.title: Unit 3 Review: Development & Learning
lessons.overview: Recap of Unit 3: cognitive development (Piaget, Vygotsky, Gibson & Walk), social/identity development (Erikson, attachment with Harlow & Ainsworth, Baumrind's parenting styles), the three types of conditioning (Pavlov, Watson & Rayner, Thorndike, Skinner, Garcia & Koelling, Tolman, Köhler, Bandura), and language development, with the Harlow practice study.
objectives: Match developmental vignettes to the correct theorist and stage.
Distinguish classical, operant, and observational learning and apply reinforcement/punishment correctly.
essentialQuestions: How do cognitive, social, and moral development unfold from infancy through adulthood?
How do classical, operant, and observational learning each change behavior, and how do you tell them apart?

source.title: The Nature of Love (contact comfort in infant monkeys, paraphrased)
source.author: Harry F. Harlow

lessons.title: Unit 4 Review: Social Psychology & Personality
lessons.overview: Recap of Unit 4: attribution and cognitive dissonance (Heider, Jones & Harris, Festinger & Carlsmith), social influence (Asch conformity, Milgram obedience, Darley & Latané bystander, Sherif, Janis), personality theories (Freud, Rogers, Costa & McCrae's Big Five, Bandura), and motivation/emotion (Yerkes, Dodson, Deci & Ryan, Baumeister & Leary, Fredrickson), with the Festinger & Carlsmith practice study.
objectives: Apply social-psychology findings (FAE, conformity, obedience, bystander effect) to scenarios.
Compare the major personality theories and recap key motivation/emotion principles using real research.
essentialQuestions: How do situations, groups, and authority shape behavior more than we expect?
How do the major personality theories explain who we are, and what drives motivation and emotion?

source.title: Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Leon Festinger & James M. Carlsmith

lessons.title: Unit 5 Review: Mental & Physical Health
lessons.overview: Recap of Unit 5: stress and health (Selye's GAS, Lazarus & Folkman, Taylor, Engel's biopsychosocial model, Felitti & Anda's ACE Study), defining/classifying disorders (DSM-5-TR; the 3 D's; Rosenhan and Cahalan's critique), the major DSM-5-TR disorder families, and treatments matched to their models (psychodynamic, humanistic/Rogers, cognitive Beck/Ellis, behavioral Wolpe, biomedical), with the Rosenhan practice study. Carries the mandatory clinical crisis strip.
objectives: Recap the stress response and the criteria/cautions for defining and classifying disorders.
Match each major treatment to its underlying model of disorder using real founders (Beck, Ellis, Wolpe, Rogers).
essentialQuestions: How does stress affect health, and how do psychologists define and classify disorders without over-pathologizing?
Which treatment matches which model of disorder (psychodynamic, humanistic, cognitive/behavioral, biomedical)?

source.title: On Being Sane in Insane Places (paraphrased)
source.author: David L. Rosenhan

lessons.title: Researcher Mega-Card Review
lessons.overview: Capstone consolidation of every CED-named researcher across Units 0 to 5, organized by unit with year + key finding, followed by a rapid-recall drill and the Bandura, Ross & Ross (1961) Bobo doll practice study with three balanced MCQs.
objectives: Connect each CED-named researcher to the correct concept, approximate year, and key finding.
Recognize researcher names rapidly in stimulus and free-response contexts and identify the study a scenario points to.
essentialQuestions: Can you connect every CED-named researcher to the right concept, year, and key finding on demand?
How do you turn 'I sort of recognize that name' into a point-earning identification on the exam?

source.title: Transmission of Aggression Through Imitation of Aggressive Models (abstract, adapted)
source.author: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross & Sheila A. Ross

lessons.title: AAQ Bootcamp: The Article Analysis Question
lessons.overview: Bootcamp on the 2025 7-point Article Analysis Question: the official A, F structure (research method, research variable/operational definition, statistic interpretation, ethical guideline, generalizability, and the 2-point argumentation part, support or refute the concept), a read-the-source drill, and a full practice AAQ on the real Sperry & Gazzaniga (1968) split-brain study.
objectives: State the six AAQ parts (A: F) and the point value of each, and explain what evidence each part requires.

Practice the AAQ on a real research source, writing complete-sentence responses that identify the method, a variable's operational definition, a statistic interpretation, an ethical guideline, generalizability, and an argument that the findings support or refute the concept.
essentialQuestions: How do I earn all 7 points on the Article Analysis Question?
How do I read a real study abstract and pull out method, variables, operationalization, generalizability, data, and a limitation?

source.title: Hemispheric Disconnection and Unity in Conscious Awareness (AAQ practice abstract)
source.author: Roger Sperry & Michael Gazzaniga

lessons.title: EBQ Bootcamp: The Evidence-Based Question
lessons.overview: Bootcamp on the 2025 7-point Evidence-Based Question (45 minutes, three summarized sources): building a defensible claim, supporting it with evidence cited from the sources, and writing reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim, practiced as one argumentative essay on a real three-source set about stress and the immune system (Cohen 1991, Selye 1956, Segerstrom & Miller 2004).
objectives: Explain how the EBQ's 7 points are earned across its three components, a defensible claim, evidence cited from the sources, and reasoning that connects the evidence to the claim, within the 45-minute window.
Practice the EBQ by drafting one claim, citing findings from three real sources, and writing reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim (optionally addressing a counter-finding).
essentialQuestions: How do I build one defensible argument that earns all 7 EBQ points in 45 minutes?
How do I cite evidence from the THREE sources and add reasoning that explains how it supports my claim?

source.title: EBQ practice: three sources on stress and the immune system
source.author: Cohen et al. (1991) · Selye (1956) · Segerstrom & Miller (2004)

lessons.title: MCQ Stamina & Strategy: The 75-Question Section
lessons.overview: Strategy clinic for the 75-item multiple-choice section: pacing math (~56 sec/item and the two-pass flag-and-move method), distractor elimination, and the three stimulus item types (concept-application, research/methods, and data/graph), with a timed mini-set built on real course studies (Pavlov, Festinger & Carlsmith, Ebbinghaus).
objectives: Calculate a per-question time budget and apply a two-pass, flag-and-move strategy with no blanks.
Eliminate distractors and correctly handle concept-application, research, and data-interpretation MCQ items.
essentialQuestions: How do I pace myself through 75 multiple-choice questions and keep my accuracy up?
How do I eliminate distractors and handle stimulus-based items (concept-application, research, and data)?

source.title: Timed MCQ practice mini-set (one of each stimulus type)
source.author: Practice items drawn from this course's content (Pavlov · Festinger · Ebbinghaus)

lessons.title: Skill Clinic: Data Interpretation & Research Design
lessons.overview: Research-skills clinic powering both the FRQs and the stimulus MCQs: reading tables/graphs, the correlation-vs-causation rule and the meaning of r, operational definitions, and validity/reliability/confounds, practiced on the real Cohen et al. (1991) stress-and-cold dose-response data.

Apply operational definitions, distinguish reliability from validity, and identify confounds that threaten a causal claim.

Why does correlation not prove causation, and how do operational definitions, validity, reliability, and confounds make or break a study?

source.title: Real-data practice, Cohen et al. (1991): stress and the common cold

Map errors to CED units/skills and build a spaced, self-testing review plan that front-loads high-yield weaknesses.
essentialQuestions: How do I turn a mock-exam score into a precise plan for what to study next?
How do I classify my errors so I fix the real problem instead of just 'studying more'?

State an FRQ time budget and an exam-day plan (preparation, materials, and prohibited items) to test calmly and strategically.

How do I budget my FRQ time and what's my day-before and day-of plan?

vocab.def: Assignment (to conditions, by chance) → causal inference; sampling (from the population, by chance) → generalizability. The single most-tested methods distinction.
A concrete, replicable statement of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
The brief all-or-none electrical impulse that travels down an axon once the stimulus passes threshold.
A drug that mimics or boosts a neurotransmitter (agonist) versus one that blocks it (antagonist).
The finding (Sperry & Gazzaniga, split-brain) that the two hemispheres are relatively specialized for different functions.
The stage of vivid dreaming with rapid eye movements and near-paralysis, discovered by Aserinsky & Kleitman (1953).
An active short-term system with a central executive directing a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad.
The principle (Craik & Lockhart 1972) that deeper, meaning-based (semantic) encoding produces stronger memory than shallow encoding.
Distortion of memory by exposure to misleading post-event information (Loftus & Palmer 1974).
Judging the likelihood of events by how readily examples come to mind (Tversky & Kahneman 1973).
The 'best,' most typical example of a category, used to judge membership (Rosch 1973).
A performance decrement caused by the fear of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group (Steele & Aronson 1995).
The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with guidance; bridged by scaffolding.
The understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight; a sensorimotor achievement (Piaget).
A structured procedure classifying infant attachment (secure vs. insecure) by reactions to caregiver separation/reunion.
REMOVING an aversive stimulus to INCREASE a behavior (not punishment).
Learning by watching and imitating a model, demonstrated in the Bobo doll study (1961).
Applying a grammatical rule too broadly ('goed'), evidence that children learn rules, not just imitate.
Overestimating disposition and underestimating the situation when explaining others' behavior (Jones & Harris 1967).
The discomfort of inconsistent attitudes/actions, which motivates attitude change to restore consistency (Festinger 1957).
The drop in felt personal obligation to act as the number of bystanders rises (Darley & Latané 1968).
The mutual interaction of behavior, personal/cognitive factors, and environment in shaping personality.
When an external reward for an already-enjoyed activity reduces intrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan).
Full acceptance of a person regardless of behavior, which supports a healthy self-concept.
The body's three-stage response to prolonged stress: alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
The view that disorders result from interacting biological, psychological, and social factors.
The American Psychiatric Association's manual (2022) defining diagnostic categories and criteria for psychological disorders.
The negative views of self, world, and future that cognitive therapy targets in depression.
A behavioral therapy pairing deep relaxation with a graded hierarchy of feared stimuli (counter-conditioning).
In schizophrenia, added experiences (hallucinations, delusions) versus losses of normal function (flat affect, avolition).
Research on patients with a severed corpus callosum revealing hemispheric specialization (Nobel 1981).
The finding that most forgetting of new material happens soon after learning, then levels off.
Overattributing others' behavior to disposition rather than situation.
IV = what the researcher manipulates/compares; DV = the outcome that is measured.
Explaining in plain English what a reported statistic or finding shows, direction and meaning, not just 'there was a difference' (AAQ Part C).
A research-ethics standard the study applied, informed consent, confidentiality, protection from harm, debriefing, the right to withdraw (AAQ Part D).
The extent to which results extend beyond the study's specific sample and setting; explained with a specific reason on AAQ Part E.
Explaining, with the source's evidence, how the findings SUPPORT or REFUTE the psychological concept being studied, the AAQ's 2-point part.
A clear, arguable thesis that directly answers the EBQ prompt and can be supported with the given sources.
An accurate finding cited from a particular source (Source A/B/C) and used to support the claim.
Explanation that makes clear HOW the cited evidence supports the claim, tying findings to the thesis (rather than just listing them).
Naming an opposing or alternative interpretation and explaining why the claim still holds, an optional but strong reasoning move.
The EBQ format: one connected essay (claim + evidence + reasoning), not a set of separately scored short-answer parts.
A pattern in which more of a variable (e.g., stress) is linked to more of an outcome (e.g., illness).
An incorrect answer option deliberately written to be plausible; eliminating distractors is the core MCQ skill.
An MCQ built on a scenario, study description, or data display that you must interpret to answer.
A question giving a real-life scenario and asking you to identify the psychological concept it illustrates.
Answering all certain items first and flagging hard ones for a second pass, to protect pacing.
A correlation shows two variables relate; it does NOT prove one causes the other (a frequent MCQ trap).
Because wrong answers aren't penalized, every question should be answered, never leave a blank.
A number from: 1.00 to +1.00 giving the direction (sign) and strength (absolute value) of a linear relationship.
One variable producing a change in another; established only by controlled experimentation, not by correlation.
The consistency of a measure across time, items, or raters.
The degree to which a measure assesses what it is intended to assess (includes internal and external validity).
An uncontrolled variable that co-varies with the independent variable and offers an alternative explanation.
Classifying each missed question by its cause (content, misread, distractor, application, timing) to target the right fix.
The finding that actively retrieving information (self-testing) improves long-term retention more than re-reading.
The finding that study distributed across time produces better retention than massed (crammed) study.
Mixing different topics/problem types within a practice session to improve discrimination and transfer.
Awareness and regulation of your own thinking and learning, the engine of an effective debrief.
A unit or skill that, given your error pattern, will gain the most points per minute of study.
The view that biological, psychological, and social-cultural factors jointly shape behavior and health (a recurring exam theme).
Classical = learning associations between stimuli (Pavlov); operant = learning from consequences (Skinner).
Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, the dominant trait model (Costa & McCrae).
Treatment targeting maladaptive thoughts and behaviors (Beck's cognitive therapy; Ellis's REBT).
Exam strategy of marking a hard MCQ, guessing, and returning later, protecting pacing across 75 items.

misconceptions: Confusing random assignment (cause) with random sampling (generalizability).
Thinking a stronger stimulus makes a 'bigger' action potential (it changes firing RATE, not size).
Treating correlation as proof of causation.
Believing memory is a faithful recording rather than a reconstruction.
Confusing the availability and representativeness heuristics.
Thinking a higher IQ test score is meaningful without standardization, reliability, and validity.
Confusing negative reinforcement with punishment.
Mixing up Piaget (cognitive stages) with Erikson (psychosocial conflicts) and Vygotsky (social scaffolding).
Thinking attachment is based on who feeds the infant (Harlow showed contact comfort matters more).
Confusing conformity (peers, Asch) with obedience (authority, Milgram).
Thinking a bigger reward always changes attitudes more (dissonance predicts the opposite for forced compliance).
Treating the fundamental attribution error and self-serving bias as the same thing.
Believing a single 'D' (just being unusual) makes behavior a disorder, rather than the combination of dysfunction, distress, and deviance.
Confusing which therapy goes with which model (e.g., assuming all therapy is 'talk about your childhood').
Taking Rosenhan's (1973) conclusions as settled fact despite Cahalan's (2019) documented concerns.
Confusing the three attachment researchers (Harlow = contact comfort; Ainsworth = attachment styles; Bowlby = theory).
Mixing up the memory researchers (Sperling = iconic; Miller = 7 ± 2; Ebbinghaus = forgetting curve; Loftus = misinformation).
Attributing a finding to the wrong member of a famous pair (e.g., Asch vs. Milgram; Festinger vs. Carlsmith's roles).
That naming a construct (e.g., 'they measured memory') satisfies Part B, the research-variable part needs the specific operational definition.
That Part F asks for a limitation or ethics, Part F is ARGUMENTATION (does the evidence SUPPORT or REFUTE the concept); the ethical guideline lives in Part D and generalizability in Part E.
That the EBQ is a set of separately scored short-answer parts, it is ONE connected argumentative essay (claim + evidence + reasoning).
That summarizing the sources is enough: evidence must be used to support an arguable claim, and reasoning must explain HOW it supports the claim.
That a 'balanced, it-depends' statement counts as a defensible claim, it usually fails to earn the claim point.
That you should leave hard questions blank, there is no guessing penalty, so always bubble an answer.
That a true statement must be the correct answer, distractors are often accurate but off-question.
That a strong correlation (large |r|) proves one variable causes the other.
That a reliable (consistent) measure must also be valid, consistency is not accuracy.
That a low score just means 'study more': without classifying error types, students often repeat the wrong fix.
That re-reading is efficient, spaced retrieval practice produces far better retention than passive review.
That an all-night cram helps, sleep consolidates memory and sustains exam-day attention; light review plus rest is better.
That phones/smartwatches are acceptable timers, they are prohibited and risk score cancellation; bring a simple watch.
